He that <hi type="italic">doeth truth</hi> is willing to know the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> by himself, and to <hi type="italic">have his deeds made manifest.</hi> A good man is much employed in trying himself, and is desirous that God would try him, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.2">Ps. xxvi. 2</reference>. He is solicitous to <hi type="italic">know</hi> what the will of God is, and resolves to <hi type="italic">do</hi> it, though ever so contrary to his own will and interest. 2. Here is the character of a <hi type="italic">good work:</hi> it is <hi type="italic">wrought in God,</hi> in union with him by a covenanting faith, and in communion with him by devout affections. Our works are <hi type="italic">then</hi> good, and will bear the test, when the will of God is the rule of them and the glory of God the end of them; when they are done in his strength, and for his sake, to him, and not to men; and if, by the light of the gospel, it be manifest to us that our works are thus wrought, <hi type="italic">then shall we have rejoicing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.4">Gal. vi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>.
entries.3a923ef3ef8928f3312db990c46ee1b8b601a1f1: <div eID="gen26817" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">John's Testimony to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen26818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> After these things came Jesus and his disciples into the land of Judæa; and there he tarried with them, and baptized. <hi type="super">23</hi> And John also was baptizing in Ænon near to Salim, because there was much water there: and they came, and were baptized. <hi type="super">24</hi> For John was not yet cast into prison. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then there arose a question between <hi type="italic">some</hi> of John's disciples and the Jews about purifying. <hi type="super">26</hi> And they came unto John, and said unto him, Rabbi, he that was with thee beyond Jordan, to whom thou barest witness, behold, the same baptizeth, and all <hi type="italic">men</hi> come to him. <hi type="super">27</hi> John answered and said, A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven. <hi type="super">28</hi> Ye yourselves bear me witness, that I said, I am not the Christ, but that I am sent before him. <hi type="super">29</hi> He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled. <hi type="super">30</hi> He must increase, but I <hi type="italic">must</hi> decrease. <hi type="super">31</hi> He that cometh from above is above all: he that is of the earth is earthly, and speaketh of the earth: he that cometh from heaven is above all. 32 And what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth; and no man receiveth his testimony. <hi type="super">33</hi> He that hath received his testimony hath set to his seal that God is true. <hi type="super">34</hi> For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God: for God giveth not the Spirit by measure <hi type="italic">unto him.</hi> <hi type="super">35</hi> The Father loveth the Son, and hath given all things into his hand. <hi type="super">36</hi> He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him. <div eID="gen26818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26819" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen26819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26820" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's removal into the land of Judea (<reference osisRef="John.3.22">v. 22</reference>), and there he tarried with his disciples. Observe, 1. Our Lord Jesus, after he entered upon his public work, travelled much, and removed often, as the patriarchs in their sojournings. As it was a good part of his humiliation that he had no certain dwelling-place, but was, as Paul, <hi type="italic">in journeyings often,</hi> so it was an instance of his unwearied industry, in the work for which he came into the world, that he went about in prosecution of it; many a weary step he took to do good to souls. The <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness</hi> took a large circuit to diffuse his light and heat, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Ps. xix. 6</reference>. 2. He was not wont to stay long at Jerusalem. Though he went frequently thither, yet he soon returned into the country; as here. <hi type="italic">After these things,</hi> after he had had this discourse with Nicodemus, he came into the land of Judea; not so much for <hi type="italic">greater privacy</hi> (though mean and obscure places best suited the humble Jesus in his humble state) as for <hi type="italic">greater usefulness.</hi> His preaching and miracles, perhaps, made <hi type="italic">most noise</hi> at Jerusalem, the fountain-head of news, but did <hi type="italic">least good</hi> there, where the most considerable men of the Jewish church had so much the ascendant. 3. When he came into the land of Judea his <hi type="italic">disciples came with him;</hi> for these were <hi type="italic">they that continued with him in his temptations.</hi> Many that flocked to him at Jerusalem could not follow his motions into the country, they had no business there; but his disciples attended him. If the ark remove, it is better to <hi type="italic">remove and go after it</hi> (as those did, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.3">Josh. iii. 3</reference>) than sit still without it, though it be in Jerusalem itself. 4. There he <hi type="italic">tarried with them,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dietribe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He conversed</hi> with them, <hi type="italic">discoursed</hi> with them. He did not retire into the country for his ease and pleasure, but for more free conversation with his disciples and followers. See <reference osisRef="Song.7.11-Song.7.12">Cant. vii. 11, 12</reference>. Note, Those that are ready to <hi type="italic">go with Christ</hi> shall find him as ready to <hi type="italic">stay with them.</hi> It is supposed that he now staid five or six months in this country. 5. There <hi type="italic">he baptized;</hi> he admitted disciples, such as believed in him, and had more honesty and courage than those had at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="John.2.42">ch. ii. 24</reference>. John began to baptize in the land of Judea (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.1">Matt. iii. 1</reference>), therefore Christ began there, for John had said, <hi type="italic">There comes one after me.</hi> He himself <hi type="italic">baptized</hi> not, with his own hand, but his disciples by his orders and directions, as appears, <reference osisRef="John.4.2">ch. iv. 2</reference>. But his disciples' baptizing was his baptizing. Holy ordinances are Christ's, though administered by weak men. <div eID="gen26820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26821" type="x-p"/> II. John's continuance in his work, as long as his opportunities lasted, <reference osisRef="John.3.23-John.3.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. Here we are told, <div eID="gen26821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26822" type="x-p"/> 1. That <hi type="italic">John was baptizing.</hi> Christ's baptism was, for substance, the same with John's, for John bore witness to Christ, and therefore they did not at all clash or interfere with one another. But, (1.) Christ began the work of preaching and baptizing before <hi type="italic">John laid it down,</hi> that he might be ready to receive John's disciples when he should be taken off, and so the wheels might be kept going. It is a comfort to useful men, when they are going off the stage, to see those rising up who are likely to fill up their place. (2.) John continued the work of preaching and baptizing though Christ had <hi type="italic">taken it up;</hi> for he would still, according to the <hi type="italic">measure given to him,</hi> advance the interests of God's kingdom. There was still work for John to do, for Christ was not yet <hi type="italic">generally known,</hi> nor were the minds of people <hi type="italic">thoroughly prepared</hi> for him by repentance. From heaven John had received his <hi type="italic">command,</hi> and he would go on in his work till he thence received his <hi type="italic">countermand,</hi> and would have his dismission from the same hand that gave him his commission. He does not <hi type="italic">come in</hi> to Christ, lest what had formerly passed should look like a combination between them; but <hi type="italic">he goes on</hi> with his work, till Providence lays him aside. The greater gifts of some do not <hi type="italic">render</hi> the labours of others, that come short of them, <hi type="italic">needless</hi> and <hi type="italic">useless;</hi> there is work enough for all hands. They are sullen that will sit down and do nothing when they see themselves out-shone. Though we have but one talent, we must account for that: and, when we see ourselves <hi type="italic">going off,</hi> must yet <hi type="italic">go on</hi> to the last. <div eID="gen26822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26823" type="x-p"/> 2. That he baptized in Enon near Salim, places we find nowhere else mentioned, and therefore the learned are altogether at a loss where to find them. Wherever it was, it seems that John removed from <hi type="italic">place to place;</hi> he did not think that there was any virtue in Jordan, because Jesus was baptized there, which should engage him to stay there, but as he saw cause he removed to other waters. Ministers must follow their opportunities. He chose a place where there was much water, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hydata polla</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">many waters,</hi> that is, many <hi type="italic">streams</hi> of water; so that wherever he met with any that were willing to submit to his baptism water was at hand to baptize them with, <hi type="italic">shallow</hi> perhaps, as is usual where there are <hi type="italic">many</hi> brooks, but such as would serve his purpose. And in that country plenty of water was a valuable thing. <div eID="gen26823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26824" type="x-p"/> 3. That thither people <hi type="italic">came to him</hi> and <hi type="italic">were baptized.</hi> Though they did not come in such vast crowds as they did when he first appeared, yet now he was not without encouragement, but there were still those that attended and owned him. Some refer this both to John and to Jesus: <hi type="italic">They came and were baptized;</hi> that is, some came to John, and were baptized by him, some to Jesus, and were baptized by him, and, as their baptism was one, so were their hearts. <div eID="gen26824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26825" type="x-p"/> 4. It is noted (<reference osisRef="John.3.24">v. 24</reference>) that <hi type="italic">John was not yet cast into prison,</hi> to clear the order of the story, and to show that these passages are to come in before <reference osisRef="Matt.6.12">Matt. vi. 12</reference>. John never desisted from his work as long as he had his liberty; nay, he seems to have been the more industrious, because he foresaw his time was short; he was not <hi type="italic">yet cast into prison,</hi> but he expected it ere long, <reference osisRef="John.9.4">ch. ix. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen26825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26826" type="x-p"/> III. A contest between <hi type="italic">John's disciples and the Jews about purifying,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.25">v. 25</reference>. See how the gospel of Christ came not to <hi type="italic">send peace upon earth,</hi> but <hi type="italic">division.</hi> Observe, 1. Who were the disputants: <hi type="italic">some of John's disciples, and the Jews</hi> who had not submitted to his baptism of repentance. Penitents and impenitents divide this sinful world. In this contest, it should seem, John's disciples were the <hi type="italic">aggressors,</hi> and gave the <hi type="italic">challenge;</hi> and it is a sign that they were novices, who had more zeal than discretion. The truths of God have often suffered by the rashness of those that have undertaken to defend them before they were able to do it. 2. What was the matter in dispute: <hi type="italic">about purifying,</hi> about <hi type="italic">religious washing.</hi> (1.) We may suppose that John's disciples cried up his baptism, his purifying, as <hi type="italic">instar omnium—superior to all others,</hi> and gave the preference to that as perfecting and superseding all the purifications of the Jews, and they were in the right; but <hi type="italic">young</hi> converts are too apt to boast of their attainments, whereas he that finds the <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> should <hi type="italic">hide it</hi> till he is sure that he has it, and not talk of it too much at first. (2.) No doubt the Jews with as much assurance applauded the <hi type="italic">purifyings</hi> that were in use among them, both those that were instituted by the law of Moses and those that were imposed by the tradition of the elders; for the former they had a divine warrant, and for the latter the usage of the church. Now it is very likely that the Jews in this dispute, when they could not <hi type="italic">deny</hi> the excellent nature and design of John's baptism, raised an objection against it from Christ's baptism, which gave occasion for the complaint that follows here (<reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>): "Here is John baptizing in one place." say they, "and Jesus at the same time baptizing in another place; and therefore John's baptism, which his disciples so much applaud, is either," [1.] "<hi type="italic">Dangerous,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">ill consequence</hi> to the peace of the church and state, for you see it opens a door to endless parties. Now that John has begun, we shall have every little teacher set up for a baptist presently. Or," [2.] "At the best it is <hi type="italic">defective</hi> and <hi type="italic">imperfect.</hi> If John's baptism, which you cry up thus, have any good in it, yonder the baptism of Jesus goes beyond it, so that for your parts you are shaded already by a greater light, and your baptism is soon gone out of request." Thus objections are made against the gospel from the advancement and improvement of gospel light, as if childhood and manhood were contrary to each other, and the superstructure were against the foundation. There was no reason to object Christ's baptism against John's, for they consisted very well together. <div eID="gen26826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26827" type="x-p"/> IV. A complaint which John's disciples made to their master concerning Christ and his baptizing, <reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>. They, being <hi type="italic">nonplussed</hi> by the fore-mentioned objection, and probably <hi type="italic">ruffled</hi> and put into a heat by it, come to their master, and tell him, "<hi type="italic">Rabbi, he that was with thee,</hi> and was baptized of thee, is now set up for himself; he <hi type="italic">baptizeth, and all men come to him;</hi> and wilt thou suffer it?" Their itch for disputing occasioned this. It is common for men, when they find themselves run aground in the heat of disputation, to fall foul upon those that do them no harm. If these disciples of John had not undertaken to dispute about <hi type="italic">purifying,</hi> before they understood the <hi type="italic">doctrine of baptism,</hi> they might have answered the objection without being put into a passion. In their complaint, they speak respectfully to their own master, <hi type="italic">Rabbit;</hi> but speak very slightly of our Saviour, though they do not name him. 1. They suggest that Christ's setting up a baptism of his own was a piece of presumption, very unaccountable; as if John, having first set up this rite of baptizing, must have the monopoly of it, and, as it were, a patent for the invention: "<hi type="italic">He that was with thee beyond Jordan,</hi> as a disciple of thine, <hi type="italic">behold,</hi> and wonder, <hi type="italic">the same,</hi> the very same, <hi type="italic">baptizes,</hi> and takes thy work out of thy hand." Thus the voluntary condescensions of the Lord Jesus, as that of his being baptized by John, are often unjustly and very unkindly turned to his reproach. 2. They suggest that it was a piece of ingratitude to John. He <hi type="italic">to whom thou barest witness</hi> baptizes; as if Jesus owed all his reputation to the honourable character John gave of him, and yet had very unworthily improved it to the prejudice of John. But Christ needed not John's testimony, <reference osisRef="John.5.36">ch. v. 36</reference>. He reflected more honour upon John than he received from him, yet thus it is incident to us to think that others are more indebted to us than really they are. And besides, Christ's baptism was not in the least an <hi type="italic">impeachment,</hi> but indeed the greatest <hi type="italic">improvement,</hi> of John's baptism, which was but to lead the way to Christ's. John was <hi type="italic">just</hi> to Christ, in bearing witness to him; and Christ's answering his testimony did rather enrich than impoverish John's ministry. 3. They conclude that it would be a total eclipse to John's baptism: "<hi type="italic">All men come to him;</hi> they that used to follow with us now flock after him, it is therefore time for us to look about us." It was not indeed strange that <hi type="italic">all men came to him.</hi> As far as Christ is <hi type="italic">manifested</hi> he will be <hi type="italic">magnified;</hi> but why should John's disciples grieve at this? Note, Aiming at the monopoly of honour and respect has been in all ages the bane of the church, and the shame of its members and ministers; as also a vying of interests, and a jealousy of rivalship and competition. We mistake if we think that the excelling gifts and graces, and labours and usefulness, of one, are a diminution and disparagement to another that has obtained mercy to be faithful; for the Spirit is a free agent, <hi type="italic">dispensing to every one severally as he will.</hi> Paul rejoiced in the usefulness even of those that <hi type="italic">opposed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.18">Phil. i. 18</reference>. We must leave it to God to choose, employ, and honour his own instruments as he pleaseth, and not covet to be <hi type="italic">placed alone.</hi> <div eID="gen26827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26828" type="x-p"/> V. Here is John's answer to this complaint which his disciples made, <reference osisRef="John.3.27">v. 27</reference>, &c. His disciples expected that he would have resented this matter as they did; but Christ's <hi type="italic">manifestation to Israel</hi> was no <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> to John, but what he looked for; it was not <hi type="italic">disturbance</hi> to him, but what he wished for. He therefore checked the complaint, as Moses, <hi type="italic">Enviest thou for my sake?</hi> and took this occasion to confirm the testimonies he had formerly borne to Christ as superior to him, cheerfully consigning and turning over to him all the interest he had in Israel. In this discourse here, the first minister of the gospel (for so John was) is an excellent pattern to all ministers to <hi type="italic">humble</hi> themselves and to <hi type="italic">exalt</hi> the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen26828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26829" type="x-p"/> 1. John here <hi type="italic">abases himself in comparison with Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.27-John.3.30">v. 27-30</reference>. The more others magnify us, the more we must humble ourselves, and fortify ourselves against the temptation of flattery and applause, and the jealousy of our friends for our honour, by remembering our place, and what we are, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">1 Cor. iii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen26829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26830" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">John acquiesces</hi> in the divine disposal, and satisfies himself with that (<reference osisRef="John.3.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">A man can receive nothing except it be given him from heaven,</hi> whence <hi type="italic">every good gift</hi> comes (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">James i. 17</reference>), a general truth very applicable in this case. Different employments are according to the direction of divine Providence, different endowments according to the distribution of the divine grace. <hi type="italic">No man can take</hi> any true <hi type="italic">honour</hi> to himself, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.4">Heb. v. 4</reference>. We have as necessary and constant a dependence upon the grace of God in all the motions and actions of the spiritual life as we have upon the providence of God in all the motions and actions of the natural life: now this comes in here as a reason, [1.] Why we should not <hi type="italic">envy</hi> those that have a larger share of gifts than we have, or move in a larger sphere of usefulness. John reminds his disciples that Jesus would not have thus excelled him <hi type="italic">except he had received it from heaven,</hi> for, as <hi type="italic">man</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mediator,</hi> he <hi type="italic">received gifts;</hi> and, if God gave him <hi type="italic">the Spirit without measure</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">v. 34</reference>), shall they grudge at it? The same reason will hold as to others. If God is <hi type="italic">pleased</hi> to give to others more ability and success than to us, shall we be displeased at it, and reflect upon him as unjust, unwise, and partial? See <reference osisRef="Matt.20.15">Matt. xx. 15</reference>. [2.] Why we should not be <hi type="italic">discontented,</hi> though we be inferior to others in gifts and usefulness, and be eclipsed by their excellencies. John was ready to own that it was the gift, the free gift, of heaven, that made him a preacher, a prophet, a baptist: it was God that gave him the interest he had in the love and esteem of the people; and, if now his interest decline, God's will be done! He that <hi type="italic">gives</hi> may <hi type="italic">take.</hi> What we <hi type="italic">receive</hi> from heaven we must take as it is <hi type="italic">given.</hi> Now John never received a commission for a standing <hi type="italic">perpetual</hi> office, but only for a <hi type="italic">temporary</hi> one, which must soon expire; and therefore, when he has fulfilled his ministry, he can contentedly see it go out of date. Some give quite another sense of these words: John had taken pains with his disciples, to teach them the reference which his baptism had to Christ, who should come after him, and yet be preferred before him, and do that for them which he could not do; and yet, after all, they dote upon John, and grudge this preference of Christ above him: Well saith John, I see <hi type="italic">a man can receive</hi> (that is, perceive) <hi type="italic">nothing, except it be given him from heaven.</hi> The labour of ministers if all lost labour, unless the grace of God make it effectual. Men do not understand that which is made most <hi type="italic">plain,</hi> nor believe that which is made most <hi type="italic">evident,</hi> unless it be given them from heaven to understand and believe it. <div eID="gen26830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26831" type="x-p"/> (2.) John appeals to the testimony he had formerly given concerning Christ (<reference osisRef="John.3.28">v. 28</reference>): You can bear me witness that I said, again and again, <hi type="italic">I am not the Christ, but I am sent before him.</hi> See how steady and constant John was in his testimony to Christ, and not as a <hi type="italic">reed shaken with the wind;</hi> neither the frowns of the chief priests, nor the flatteries of his own disciples, could make him change his note. Now this serves here, [1.] As a <hi type="italic">conviction</hi> to his disciples of the unreasonableness of their complaint. They had spoken of the witness which their master bore to Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>): "Now," saith John, "do you not remember what the testimony was that I did bear? Call that to mind, and you will see your own cavil answered. Did I not say, <hi type="italic">I am not the Christ?</hi> Why then do you set me up as a rival with him that is? Did I not say, <hi type="italic">I am sent before him?</hi> Why then does it seem strange to you that I should stand by and give way to him?" [2.] It is a <hi type="italic">comfort</hi> to himself that he had never <hi type="italic">given</hi> his disciples <hi type="italic">any occasion</hi> thus to set him up in competition with Christ; but, on the contrary, had particularly <hi type="italic">cautioned</hi> them against this mistake, though he might have made a hand of it for himself. It is a satisfaction to faithful ministers when they have done what they could in their places to prevent any extravagances that their people ran into. John had not only not encouraged them to hope that he was the Messiah, but had plainly told them the contrary, which was now a satisfaction to him. It is a common excuse for those who have undue honour paid them, <hi type="italic">Si populus vult decipi, decipiatur—If the people will be deceived, let them;</hi> but that is an ill maxim for those to go by whose business it is to <hi type="italic">undeceive</hi> people. <hi type="italic">The lip of truth shall be established.</hi> <div eID="gen26831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26832" type="x-p"/> (3.) John professes the great satisfaction he had in the advancement of Christ and his interest. He was so far from <hi type="italic">regretting</hi> it, as his disciples did, that he <hi type="italic">rejoiced</hi> in it. This he expresses (<reference osisRef="John.3.29">v. 29</reference>) by an elegant similitude. [1.] He compares our Saviour to the <hi type="italic">bridegroom: "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom.</hi> Do <hi type="italic">all men come to him?</hi> It is well, whither else should they go? Has he got the throne in men's affections? Who else should have it? It is his right; to whom should the bride be brought but to the bridegroom?" Christ was prophesied of in the Old Testament as a bridegroom, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17">Ps. xlv</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Word was made flesh,</hi> that the disparity of nature might not be a <hi type="italic">bar to the match.</hi> Provision is made for the purifying of the church, that the defilement of sin might be no bar. Christ espouses his church to himself; he <hi type="italic">has</hi> the bride, for he has her love, he has her promise; <hi type="italic">the church is subject to Christ.</hi> As far as particular souls are devoted to him in faith and love, so far the bridegroom has the bride. [2.] He compares himself to the <hi type="italic">friend of the bridegroom,</hi> who attends upon him, to do him honour and service, assists him in prosecuting the match, speaks a good word for him, uses his interest on his behalf, rejoices when the match goes on, and most of all when the point is gained, and he <hi type="italic">has the bride.</hi> All that John had done in preaching and baptizing was to introduce him; and, now that he was come, he had what he wished for: <hi type="italic">The friend of the bridegroom stands, and hears him;</hi> stands expecting him, and waiting for him; <hi type="italic">rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom's voice,</hi> because he is come to the marriage after he had been long expected. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Faithful ministers are friends of the bridegroom, to recommend him to the affections and choice of the children of men; to bring letters and messages from him, for he courts by proxy; and herein they must be faithful to him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The friends of the bridegroom must <hi type="italic">stand, and hear the bridegroom's voice;</hi> must receive instructions from him, and attend his orders; must desire to have proofs of Christ speaking in them, and with them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.3">2 Cor. xiii. 3</reference>); that is the <hi type="italic">bridegroom's voice. Thirdly,</hi> The espousing of souls to Jesus Christ, in faith and love, is the fulfilling of the joy of every good minister. If the day of Christ's espousals be the day of the gladness of his heart (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">Cant. iii. 11</reference>), it cannot but be of their too who love him and wish well to his honour and kingdom. Surely they have <hi type="italic">no greater joy.</hi> <div eID="gen26832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26833" type="x-p"/> (4.) He owns it highly fit and necessary that the reputation and interest of Christ should be advanced, and his own diminished (<reference osisRef="John.3.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">He must increase, but I must decrease.</hi> If they grieve at the growing greatness of the Lord Jesus, they will have more and more occasion to grieve, as those have that indulge themselves in envy and emulation. John speaks of Christ's increase and his own decrease, not only as <hi type="italic">necessary</hi> and <hi type="italic">unavoidable,</hi> which could not be <hi type="italic">helped</hi> and therefore must be <hi type="italic">borne,</hi> but as highly <hi type="italic">just</hi> and <hi type="italic">agreeable,</hi> and affording him entire satisfaction. [1.] He was <hi type="italic">well pleased</hi> to see the kingdom of Christ getting ground: "<hi type="italic">He must increase.</hi> You think he has gained a great deal, but it is nothing to what he will gain." Note, The kingdom of Christ is, and will be, a growing kingdom, like the light of the morning, like the grain of mustard-seed. [2.] He was not at all <hi type="italic">displeased</hi> that the effect of this was the diminishing of his own interest: <hi type="italic">I must decrease.</hi> Created excellencies are under this law, they <hi type="italic">must decrease. I have seen an end of all perfection.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The shining forth of the glory of Christ eclipses the lustre of all other glory. The glory that stands in <hi type="italic">competition</hi> with Christ, that of the world and the flesh, decreases and loses ground in the soul as the knowledge and love of Christ increase and get ground; but it is here spoken of that which is <hi type="italic">subservient</hi> to him. As the light of the morning increases, that of the morning star decreases. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> If our diminution or abasement may but in the least contribute to the advancement of Christ's name, we must cheerfully submit to it, and be content to be <hi type="italic">any thing,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">nothing,</hi> so that Christ may be <hi type="italic">all.</hi> <div eID="gen26833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26834" type="x-p"/> 2. John Baptist here <hi type="italic">advances</hi> Christ, and instructs his disciples concerning him, that, instead of grieving that so many come to him, they might come to him themselves. <div eID="gen26834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26835" type="x-p"/> (1.) He instructs them concerning the <hi type="italic">dignity of Christ's person</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that cometh from above,</hi> that <hi type="italic">cometh from heaven, is above all.</hi> Here, [1.] He supposes his divine origin, that he came <hi type="italic">from above,</hi> from <hi type="italic">heaven,</hi> which bespeaks not only his divine extraction, but his divine nature. He had a being before his conception, a heavenly being. None but he that came from heaven was fit to show us the will of heaven, or the way to heaven. When God would save man, he <hi type="italic">sent from above.</hi> [2.] Hence he infers his sovereign authority: he is <hi type="italic">above all,</hi> above all things and all persons, <hi type="italic">God over all, blessed for evermore.</hi> It is daring presumption to dispute precedency with him. When we come to speak of the honours of the Lord Jesus, we find they transcend all conception and expression, and we can say but this, <hi type="italic">He is above all.</hi> It was said of John Baptist, <hi type="italic">There is not a greater among them that are born of women.</hi> But the descent of Christ from heaven put such a dignity upon him as he was not divested of by his being made flesh; still he was <hi type="italic">above all.</hi> This he further illustrates by the meanness of those who stood in competition with him: <hi type="italic">He that is of the earth, is earthly,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho on ek tes ges, ek tes ges esti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He that is of the earth is of the earth;</hi> he that has his origin of the earth has his food out of the earth, has his converse with earthly things, and his concern is for them. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Man has his rise out of the earth; not only Adam at first, but we also still are <hi type="italic">formed out of the clay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job xxxiii. 6</reference>. Look to the rock whence we were hewn. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Man's constitution is therefore <hi type="italic">earthly;</hi> not only his body frail and mortal, but his soul corrupt and carnal, and its bent and bias strong towards earthly things. The prophets and apostles were of the same mould with other men; they were but <hi type="italic">earthen vessels,</hi> though they had a rich treasure lodged in them; and shall these be set up as rivals with Christ? <hi type="italic">Let the potsherds strive with the potsherds of the earth;</hi> but let them not cope with him that <hi type="italic">came from heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen26835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26836" type="x-p"/> (2.) Concerning the <hi type="italic">excellency and certainty of his doctrine.</hi> His disciples were displeased that Christ's preaching was admired, and attended upon, more than his; but he tells them that there was reason enough for it. For, <div eID="gen26836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26837" type="x-p"/> [1.] He, for his part, <hi type="italic">spoke of the earth,</hi> and so do all those that are <hi type="italic">of the earth.</hi> The prophets were men and spoke like men; <hi type="italic">of themselves</hi> they could not speak but <hi type="italic">of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2 Cor. iii. 5</reference>. The preaching of the prophets and of John was but low and flat compared with Christ's preaching; as heaven is high above the earth, so were his thoughts above theirs. By them God spoke <hi type="italic">on earth,</hi> but in Christ he speaketh <hi type="italic">from heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen26837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26838" type="x-p"/> [2.] But he that cometh from heaven is not only in his person, but in his doctrine, above all the prophets that ever lived on earth; none teacheth like him. The doctrine of Christ is here recommended to us, <div eID="gen26838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26839" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As infallibly <hi type="italic">sure</hi> and <hi type="italic">certain,</hi> and to be entertained accordingly (<reference osisRef="John.3.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">What he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth.</hi> See here, 1. Christ's divine knowledge; he testified nothing but <hi type="italic">what he had seen and heard,</hi> what he was perfectly apprized of and thoroughly acquainted with. What he discovered of the divine nature and of the invisible world was what he had <hi type="italic">seen;</hi> what he revealed of the mind of God was what he had <hi type="italic">heard</hi> immediately from him, and not at second hand. The prophets testified what was made known to them in creams and visions by the mediation of angels, but not what they had seen and heard. John was the crier's <hi type="italic">voice,</hi> that said, "<hi type="italic">Make room for the witness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">keep silence</hi> while the charge is given," but then leaves it to the witness to give in his testimony himself, and the judge to give the charge himself. The gospel of Christ is not a doubtful opinion, like an hypothesis or new notion in philosophy, which every one is at liberty to believe or not; but it is a revelation of the mind of God, which is of <hi type="italic">eternal truth</hi> in itself, and of <hi type="italic">infinite concern</hi> to us. 2. His divine grace and goodness: that which he had <hi type="italic">seen</hi> and <hi type="italic">heard</hi> he was pleased to make known to us, because he knew it nearly concerned us. What Paul had seen and heard in the third heavens he could not testify (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">2 Cor. xii. 4</reference>), but Christ knew how to utter what he had <hi type="italic">seen</hi> and <hi type="italic">heard.</hi> Christ's preaching is here called his <hi type="italic">testifying,</hi> to denote, (1.) The <hi type="italic">convincing evidence</hi> of it; it was not <hi type="italic">reported</hi> as news by hearsay, but it was <hi type="italic">testified</hi> as evidence given in court, with great caution and assurance. (2.) The affectionate earnestness of the delivery of it: it was testified with concern and importunity, as <reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Acts xviii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen26839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26840" type="x-p"/> From the <hi type="italic">certainty</hi> of Christ's doctrine, John takes occasion, [1.] To lament the infidelity of the most of men: though he testifies what is infallibly true, yet <hi type="italic">no man re</hi>ceiveth his testimony, that is, very few, next to none, none in comparison with those that refuse it. They receive it not, they will not hear it, they do not heed it, or give credit to it. This he speaks of not only as a matter of <hi type="italic">wonder,</hi> that such a testimony should not be received (Who hath believed our report? How stupid and foolish are the greatest part of mankind, what enemies to themselves!) but as matter of <hi type="italic">grief;</hi> John's disciples grieved that <hi type="italic">all men came to Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>); they thought his followers too many. But John grieves that <hi type="italic">no man came to him;</hi> he thought them too few. Note, The unbelief of sinners is the grief of saints. It was for this that St. Paul had <hi type="italic">great heaviness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.2">Rom. ix. 2</reference>. [2.] He takes occasion to commend the faith of the chosen remnant (<reference osisRef="John.3.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that hath received his testimony</hi> (and some such there were, though very few) hath <hi type="italic">set to his seal that God is true.</hi> God is true, though we do not <hi type="italic">set our seal to it;</hi> let God be true, and every man a liar; his truth needs not our faith to support it, but by faith we do ourselves the honour and justice to subscribe to his truth, and hereby God reckons himself honoured. God's promises are all <hi type="italic">yea and amen;</hi> by faith we put our <hi type="italic">amen</hi> to them, as <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Rev. xxii. 20</reference>. Observe, He that receives the testimony of Christ subscribes not only to the truth of Christ, but to the truth of <hi type="italic">God,</hi> for his name is the <hi type="italic">Word of God;</hi> the commandments of God and the testimony of Christ are put together, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.17">Rev. xii. 17</reference>. By believing in Christ we set to our seal, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That God is true to all the promises which he has made <hi type="italic">concerning Christ,</hi> that which he spoke by the mouth of <hi type="italic">all his holy prophets;</hi> what he <hi type="italic">swore to our fathers</hi> is all accomplished, and not one iota or tittle of it fallen to the ground, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.70 Acts.13.32-Acts.13.33">Luke i. 70, &c. Acts xiii. 32, 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he is true to all the promises he has made <hi type="italic">in Christ;</hi> we venture our souls upon God's veracity, being satisfied that he is <hi type="italic">true;</hi> we are willing to deal with him <hi type="italic">upon trust,</hi> and to quit all in this world for a happiness in reversion and out of sight. By this we greatly honour God's faithfulness. Whom we <hi type="italic">give credit</hi> to we <hi type="italic">give honour</hi> to. <div eID="gen26840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26841" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is recommended to us as a <hi type="italic">divine</hi> doctrine; not his own, but <hi type="italic">his that sent</hi> him (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">For he whom God hath sent speaketh the word of God,</hi> which he was sent to speak, and enabled to speak; <hi type="italic">for God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him.</hi> The prophets were as messengers that brought letters from heaven; but Christ came under the character of an <hi type="italic">ambassador,</hi> and treats with us as such; for, 1. He spoke the <hi type="italic">words of God,</hi> and nothing he said savoured of human infirmity; both substance and language were divine. He proved himself <hi type="italic">sent of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.2">ch. iii. 2</reference>), and therefore his words are to be received as the words of God. By this rule we may try the spirits: those that speak <hi type="italic">as the oracles of God,</hi> and prophesy <hi type="italic">according to the proportion of faith,</hi> are to be received as <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> 2. He spoke as no other prophet did; for <hi type="italic">God giveth not the Spirit by measure to him.</hi> None can speak the <hi type="italic">words of God</hi> without the <hi type="italic">Spirit of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10-1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 10, 11</reference>. The Old-Testament prophets had the Spirit, and in different degrees, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.9-2Kgs.2.10">2 Kings ii. 9, 10</reference>. But, whereas God gave them the Spirit by <hi type="italic">measure</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1 Cor. xii. 4</reference>), he gave him to Christ <hi type="italic">without measure;</hi> all fulness dwelt in him, the fulness of the Godhead, an immeasurable fulness. The Spirit was not in Christ as in a vessel, but as in a fountain, as in a bottomless ocean. "The prophets that had the Spirit in a limited manner, only with respect to some particular revelation, sometimes spoke of <hi type="italic">themselves;</hi> but he that had the Spirit always residing in him, without stint, always spoke <hi type="italic">the words of God.</hi>" So Dr. Whitby. <div eID="gen26841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26842" type="x-p"/> (3.) Concerning <hi type="italic">the power and authority he is invested with,</hi> which gives him the pre-eminence above all others, and a more excellent name than they. <div eID="gen26842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26843" type="x-p"/> [1.] He is the <hi type="italic">beloved Son of the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Father loveth the Son.</hi> The prophets were faithful as servants, but Christ as a Son; they were employed as servants, but Christ <hi type="italic">beloved</hi> as a son, always <hi type="italic">his delight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. The Father was well pleased in him; not only he <hi type="italic">did</hi> love him, but he <hi type="italic">doth</hi> love him; he continued his love to him even in his estate of humiliation, loved him never the less for his poverty and sufferings. <div eID="gen26843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26844" type="x-p"/> [2.] He is <hi type="italic">Lord of all.</hi> The Father, as an evidence of his love for him, <hi type="italic">hath given all things into his hand.</hi> Love is generous. The Father took such a complacency and had such a confidence in him that he constituted him the great <hi type="italic">feoffee in trust</hi> for mankind. Having given <hi type="italic">him the Spirit without measure,</hi> he gave him <hi type="italic">all things;</hi> for he was hereby qualified to be master and manager of all. Note, It is the honour of Christ, and the unspeakable comfort of all Christians, that the Father hath <hi type="italic">given all things</hi> into the hands of the Mediator. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> All <hi type="italic">power;</hi> so it is explained, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Matt. xxviii. 18</reference>. All the works of creation being put under his feet, all the affairs of redemption are put into his hand; he is Lord of all. Angels are his servants; devils are his captives. He has <hi type="italic">power over all flesh,</hi> the <hi type="italic">heathen</hi> given <hi type="italic">him for his inheritance.</hi> The kingdom of providence is committed to his administration. He has power to settle the terms of the covenant of peace as the great <hi type="italic">plenipotentiary,</hi> to govern his church as the great <hi type="italic">lawgiver,</hi> to dispense divine favours as the great <hi type="italic">almoner,</hi> and to call all to account as the great <hi type="italic">Judge.</hi> Both the golden sceptre and the iron rod are given into his hand. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> All <hi type="italic">grace</hi> is given into his hand as the channel of conveyance; <hi type="italic">all things,</hi> all those good things which God intended to give to the children of men; <hi type="italic">eternal life,</hi> and all its preliminaries. We are unworthy that the Father should give those things <hi type="italic">into our hands,</hi> for we have made ourselves the <hi type="italic">children of his wrath;</hi> he hath therefore appointed the <hi type="italic">Son of his love</hi> to be trustee for us, and the things he intended for us he gives <hi type="italic">into his hands,</hi> who is worthy, and has merited both honours for himself and favours for us. They are given <hi type="italic">into his hands,</hi> by him to be given into ours. This is a great encouragement to faith, that the riches of the new covenant are deposited in so sure, so kind, so good a hand, the hand of him that purchased them for us, and us for himself, who is able to keep all that which both God and believers have agreed to <hi type="italic">commit to him.</hi> <div eID="gen26844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26845" type="x-p"/> [3.] He is the object of that faith which is made the great condition of eternal happiness, and herein he has the pre-eminence above all others: <hi type="italic">He that believeth on the Son, hath life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.36">v. 36</reference>. We have here the application of what he had said concerning Christ and his doctrine; and it is the <hi type="italic">conclusion of the whole matter.</hi> If God has put this honour upon the Son, we must by faith give honour to him. As God offers and conveys good things to us by the <hi type="italic">testimony</hi> of Jesus Christ, whose word is the vehicle of divine favours, so we receive and partake of those favours by <hi type="italic">believing</hi> the testimony, and entertaining that word as <hi type="italic">true</hi> and <hi type="italic">good;</hi> this way of <hi type="italic">receiving</hi> fitly answers that way of <hi type="italic">giving.</hi> We have here the sum of that gospel which is to be preached to every creature, <reference osisRef="Mark.16.16">Mark xvi. 16</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen26845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The blessed state of all true Christians: <hi type="italic">He that believes on the Son hath everlasting life.</hi> Note, 1. It is the character of every true Christian that he believes on <hi type="italic">the Son of God;</hi> not only <hi type="italic">believes him,</hi> that what he saith is true, but believes <hi type="italic">on him,</hi> consents to him, and confides in him. The benefit of true Christianity is no less than <hi type="italic">everlasting life;</hi> this is what Christ came to purchase for us and confer upon us; it can be no less than the happiness of an immortal soul <hi type="italic">in</hi> an immortal God. 2. True believers, even now, <hi type="italic">have</hi> everlasting life; not only they shall have it hereafter, but they have it now. For, (1.) They <hi type="italic">have</hi> very good security for it. The deed by which it passeth is sealed and delivered to them, and so they <hi type="italic">have</hi> it; it is put into the hands of their guardian for them, and so they have it, though the use be not yet transferred into possession. They have the Son of God, and in him <hi type="italic">they have life;</hi> and the Spirit of God, the earnest of this life. (2.) They have the comfortable <hi type="italic">foretastes</hi> of it, in present communion with God and the tokens of his love. Grace is glory begun.  <chapter eID="John.3"/> <div eID="gen26846" type="x-p"/>

entries.cb6bf6e377f2862ba2db2937af098cbaddc2a71b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14890"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.3.1-John.3.21">Joh 3:1-21</reference>. Night Interview of Nicodemus with Jesus.</title> <div sID="gen28739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14890"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Nicodemus--</hi>In this member of the Sanhedrim sincerity and timidity are seen struggling together. <div eID="gen28739" type="x-p"/>
entries.10eb4bb98c9677448a58dadd80752cc3f3669f1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14892"/><div sID="gen28742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14892"/><hi type="bold">3. Except, &c.--</hi>This blunt and curt reply was plainly meant to shake the whole edifice of the man's religion, in order to lay a deeper and more enduring foundation. Nicodemus probably thought he had gone a long way, and expected, perhaps, to be complimented on his candor. Instead of this, he is virtually told that he has raised a question which he is not in a capacity to solve, and that before approaching it, his spiritual vision required to be rectified by an entire revolution on his inner man. Had the man been less sincere, this would certainly have repelled him; but with persons in his mixed state of mind--to which Jesus was no stranger (<reference osisRef="John.2.25">Joh 2:25</reference>)--such methods speed better than more honeyed words and gradual approaches.<div eID="gen28742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man--</hi>not a Jew merely; the necessity is a universal one.<div eID="gen28743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be born again--</hi>or, as it were, begin life anew in relation to God; his manner of thinking, feeling, and acting, with reference to spiritual things, undergoing a fundamental and permanent revolution.<div eID="gen28744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot see--</hi>can have no part in (just as one is said to "see life," "see death," &c.).<div eID="gen28745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the kingdom of God--</hi>whether in its beginnings here (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Lu 16:16</reference>), or its consummation hereafter (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">Mt 25:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>). <div eID="gen28746" type="x-p"/>
entries.db7f935b36252807c54a895a17cfe37eae874b71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14893"/><div sID="gen28747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14893"/><hi type="bold">4. How, &c.--</hi>The figure of the new birth, if it had been meant only of Gentile proselytes to the Jewish religion, would have been intelligible enough to Nicodemus, being quite in keeping with the language of that day; but that Jews themselves should need a new birth was to him incomprehensible. <div eID="gen28747" type="x-p"/>
entries.5927912716e4f91946f4ff891abb6ea1324d4449: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14894"/><div sID="gen28748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14894"/><hi type="bold">5. of water and of the Spirit--</hi>A twofold explanation of the "new birth," so startling to Nicodemus. To a Jewish ecclesiastic, so familiar with the symbolical application of water, in every variety of way and form of expression, this language was fitted to show that the thing intended was no other than a thorough spiritual purification by the operation of the Holy Ghost. Indeed, element of water and operation of the Spirit are brought together in a glorious evangelical prediction of Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25-Ezek.36.27">Eze 36:25-27</reference>), which Nicodemus might have been reminded of had such spiritualities not been almost lost in the reigning formalism. Already had the symbol of water been embodied in an initiatory ordinance, in the baptism of the Jewish expectants of Messiah by the Baptist, not to speak of the baptism of Gentile proselytes before that; and in the Christian Church it was soon to become the great visible door of entrance into "the kingdom of God," the reality being the sole work of the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>). <div eID="gen28748" type="x-p"/>
entries.48edde0fa46dbd3875d339c682545bd16c6ee8c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14895"/><div sID="gen28749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14895"/><hi type="bold">6-8. That which is born, &c.--</hi>A great universal proposition; "That which is begotten carries within itself the nature of that which begat it" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen28749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>Not the mere material body, but all that comes into the world by birth, the entire man; yet not humanity simply, but in its corrupted, depraved condition, in complete subjection to the law of the fall (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.1-Rom.8.9">Ro 8:1-9</reference>). So that though a man "could enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born," he would be no nearer this "new birth" than before (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">Job 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.5">Psa 51:5</reference>).<div eID="gen28750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is spirit--</hi>"partakes of and possesses His spiritual nature." <div eID="gen28751" type="x-p"/>
entries.67686775a0015607fffff1ba1b2bce33c227f1d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14898"/><div sID="gen28756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14898"/><hi type="bold">9-10. How, &c.--</hi>Though the subject still confounds Nicodemus, the necessity and possibility of the new birth is no longer the point with him, but the nature of it and how it is brought about [Luthardt]. "From this moment Nicodemus says nothing more, but has sunk unto a disciple who has found his true teacher. Therefore the Saviour now graciously advances in His communications of truth, and once more solemnly brings to the mind of this teacher in Israel, now become a learner, his own not guiltless ignorance, that He may then proceed to utter, out of the fulness of His divine knowledge, such farther testimonies both of earthly and heavenly things as his docile scholar may to his own profit receive" [Stier]. <div eID="gen28756" type="x-p"/>
entries.4216c13bb15d2b3a3c9fa4d1f343cace18c0b03e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14900"/><div sID="gen28758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14900"/><hi type="bold">11-13. We speak that we know, and ... have seen--</hi>that is, by absolute knowledge and immediate vision of God, which "the only-begotten Son in the bosom of the Father" claims as exclusively His own (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>). The "we" and "our" are here used, though Himself only is intended, in emphatic contrast, probably, with the opening words of Nicodemus, "Rabbi, we know.", &c.<div eID="gen28758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye receive not, &c.--</hi>referring to the class to which Nicodemus belonged, but from which he was beginning to be separated in spirit. <div eID="gen28759" type="x-p"/>
entries.9044b8cfbc41545b256ef62ac1ab965789167d90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14903"/><div sID="gen28763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14903"/><hi type="bold">14-16. And as Moses, &c.--</hi>Here now we have the "heavenly things," as before the "earthly," but under a veil, for the reason mentioned in <reference osisRef="John.3.12">Joh 3:12</reference>. The crucifixion of Messiah is twice after this veiled under the same lively term--"uplifting," <reference osisRef="John.8.28">Joh 8:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.32">12:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.33">33</reference>. Here it is still further veiled--though to us who know what it means, rendered vastly more instructive--by reference to the brazen serpent. The venom of the fiery serpents, shooting through the veins of the rebellious Israelites, was spreading death through the camp--lively emblem of the perishing condition of men by reason of sin. In both cases the remedy was divinely provided. In both the way of cure strikingly resembled that of the disease. Stung by serpents, by a serpent they are healed. By "fiery serpents" bitten--serpents, probably, with skin spotted fiery red [Kurtz]--the instrument of cure is a serpent of brass or copper, having at a distance the same appearance. So in redemption, as by man came death, by Man also comes life--Man, too, "in the likeness of sinful flesh" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Ro 8:3</reference>), differing in nothing outward and apparent from those who, pervaded by the poison of the serpent, were ready to perish. But as the uplifted serpent had none of the venom of which the serpent-bitten people were dying, so while the whole human family were perishing of the deadly wound inflicted on it by the old serpent, "the Second Man," who arose over humanity with healing in His wings, was without spot or wrinkle, or any such thing. In both cases the remedy is conspicuously displayed; in the one case on a pole, in the other on the cross, to "draw all men unto Him" (<reference osisRef="John.12.32">Joh 12:32</reference>). In both cases it is by directing the eye to the uplifted Remedy that the cure is effected; in the one case the bodily eye, in the other the gaze of the soul by "believing in Him," as in that glorious ancient proclamation--"Look unto me and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.22">Is 45:22</reference>). Both methods are stumbling to human reason. What, to any thinking Israelite, could seem more unlikely than that a deadly poison should be dried up in his body by simply looking on a reptile of brass? Such a stumbling-block to the Jews and to the Greeks foolishness was faith in the crucified Nazarene as a way of deliverance from eternal perdition. Yet was the warrant in both cases to expect a cure equally rational and well grounded. As the serpent was God's ordinance for the cure of every bitten Israelite, so is Christ for the salvation of every perishing sinner--the one however a purely arbitrary ordinance, the other divinely adapted to man's complicated maladies. In both cases the efficacy is the same. As one simple look at the serpent, however distant and however weak, brought an instantaneous cure, even so, real faith in the Lord Jesus, however tremulous, however distant--be it but real faith--brings certain and instant healing to the perishing soul. In a word, the consequences of disobedience are the same in both. Doubtless many bitten Israelites, galling as their case was, would reason rather than obey, would speculate on the absurdity of expecting the bite of a living serpent to be cured by looking at a piece of dead metal in the shape of one--speculate thus till they died. Alas! is not salvation by a crucified Redeemer subjected to like treatment? Has the offense of the cross" yet ceased? (Compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.12">2Ki 5:12</reference>). <div eID="gen28763" type="x-p"/>
entries.987d91dbe69f50d6c46e27adfca927ca80dba83f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14905"/><div sID="gen28765" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14905"/><hi type="bold">17-21. not to condemn, &c.--</hi>A statement of vast importance. Though "condemnation" is to many the issue of Christ's mission (<reference osisRef="John.3.19">Joh 3:19</reference>), it is not the object of His mission, which is purely a saving one. <div eID="gen28765" type="x-p"/>
entries.b622b1f0a8f561dcea41f8080f18641b4332fbee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14910"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.3.22-John.3.36">Joh 3:22-36</reference>. Jesus in the Neighborhood of the Baptist--His Noble Testimony to His Master.</title> <div sID="gen28773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14910"/><hi type="bold">22-24. land of Judea--</hi>the rural parts of that province, the foregoing conversation being held in the capital.<div eID="gen28773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">baptized--</hi>in the sense explained in <reference osisRef="John.4.2">Joh 4:2</reference>. <div eID="gen28774" type="x-p"/>
entries.2feb07bb462f919d2bb79d9629e068f5c4202a5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14913"/><div sID="gen28777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14913"/><hi type="bold">25-26. between some of--</hi>rather, "on the part of."<div eID="gen28777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the Jews--</hi>rather (according to the best manuscripts), "and a Jew,"<div eID="gen28778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">about purifying--</hi>that is, baptizing, the symbolical meaning of washing with water being put (as in <reference osisRef="John.2.6">Joh 2:6</reference>) for the act itself. As John and Jesus were the only teachers who baptized Jews, discussions might easily arise between the Baptist's disciples and such Jews as declined to submit to that rite. <div eID="gen28779" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b55b52dd1dfa6c60257684cf2b5db6428b3ffde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14915"/><div sID="gen28781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14915"/><hi type="bold">27-30. A man, &c.--</hi>"I do my heaven-prescribed work, and that is enough for me. Would you have me mount into my Master's place? Said I not unto you, I am not the Christ? The Bride is not mine, why should the people stay with me?? Mine it is to point the burdened to the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world, to tell them there is Balm in Gilead, and a Physician there. And shall I grudge to see them, in obedience to the call, flying as a cloud, and as doves to their windows? Whose is the Bride but the Bridegroom's? Enough for me to be the Bridegroom's friend, sent by Him to negotiate the match, privileged to bring together the Saviour and those He is come to seek and to save, and rejoicing with joy unspeakable if I may but 'stand and hear the Bridegroom's voice,' witnessing the blessed espousals. Say ye, then, they go from me to Him? Ye bring me glad tidings of great joy. He must increase, but I must decrease; this, my joy, therefore is fulfilled."<div eID="gen28781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">A man can receive, &c.--</hi>assume nothing, that is, lawfully and with any success; that is, Every man has his work and sphere appointed him from above, Even Christ Himself came under this law (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.4">He 5:4</reference>). <div eID="gen28782" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdc7c82c99c1a6521c4066f22357b3e179d3fc3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14916"/><div sID="gen28783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14916"/><hi type="bold">31-34. He that, &c.--</hi>Here is the reason why He must increase while all human teachers must decrease. The Master "cometh from above"--descending from His proper element, the region of those "heavenly things" which He came to reveal, and so, although mingling with men and things on the earth, is not "of the earth," either in Person or Word. The servants, on the contrary, springing of earth, are of the earth, and their testimony, even though divine in authority, partakes necessarily of their own earthiness. (So strongly did the Baptist feel this contrast that the last clause just repeats the first). It is impossible for a sharper line of distinction to be drawn between Christ and all human teachers, even when divinely commissioned and speaking by the power of the Holy Ghost. And who does not perceive it? The words of prophets and apostles are undeniable and most precious truth; but in the words of Christ we hear a voice as from the excellent Glory, the Eternal Word making Himself heard in our own flesh. <div eID="gen28783" type="x-p"/>
entries.c226b9610a1c355eac83461f31784b83104d173b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14920"/><div sID="gen28788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14920"/><hi type="bold">35-36. The Father loveth, &c.--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Mt 11:27</reference>, where we have the "delivering over of all things into the hands of the Son," while here we have the deep spring of that august act in the Father's ineffable "love of the Son." <div eID="gen28788" type="x-p"/>

entries.069aca9d9273881da4e05f110d50ad0556ee32d8: <div eID="gen41511" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen41512" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41513" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41513" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41512" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41514" type="x-p"/> The conversation between Nicodemus and our Lord, about the new birth and faith in his testimony, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.1-Joh.3.15">Joh 3:1-15</reference>. The love of God, the source of human salvation, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>. Who are condemned, and who are approved, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.17-Joh.3.21">Joh 3:17-21</reference>. Jesus and his disciples come to Judea, and baptize, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.22">Joh 3:22</reference>. John baptizes in Aenon, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.23">Joh 3:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.24">Joh 3:24</reference>. The disciples of John and the Pharisees dispute about purifying, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.25">Joh 3:25</reference>. The discourse between John and his disciples about Christ, in which the excellence, perfection, and privileges, of the Christian dispensation are pointed out, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.26-Joh.3.36">Joh 3:26-36</reference>. <div eID="gen41514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41515" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen41515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41516" type="x-p"/> Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews - One of the members of the grand Sanhedrin; for such were ordinarily styled rulers among the Jews. A person of the name of Nicodemus, the son of Gorion, is mentioned in the Jewish writings, who lived in the time of Vespasian, and was reputed to be so rich that he could support all the inhabitants of Jerusalem for ten years. But this is said in their usual extravagant mode of talking.
entries.b540d580aea5d402a4840dbf2745ed0ac2be0c26: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen41516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41517" type="x-p"/> Came to Jesus by night - He had matters of the utmost importance, on which he wished to consult Christ; and he chose the night season, perhaps less through the fear of man than through a desire to have Jesus alone, as he found him all the day encompassed with the multitude; so that it was impossible for him to get an opportunity to speak fully on those weighty affairs concerning which he intended to consult him. However, we may take it for granted that he had no design at present to become his disciple; as baptism and circumcision, which were the initiating ordinances among the Jews, were never administered in the night time. If any person received baptism by night, he was not acknowledged for a proselyte. See Wetstein. But as Jews were not obliged to be baptized, they being circumcised, and consequently in the covenant, he, being a Jew, would not feel any necessity of submitting to this rite. <div eID="gen41517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41518" type="x-p"/> Rabbi - My Master, or Teacher, a title of respect given to the Jewish doctors, something like our Doctor of Divinity, i.e. teacher of Divine things. But as there may be many found among us who, though they bear the title, are no teachers, so it was among the Jews; and perhaps it was in reference to this that Nicodemus uses the word διδασκαλος, didaskalos, immediately after, by which, in <reference osisRef="Joh.1.38">Joh 1:38</reference>, St. John translates the word rabbi. Rabbi, teacher, is often no more than a title of respect: didaskolos signifies a person who not only has the name of teacher, but who actually does teach. <div eID="gen41518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41519" type="x-p"/> We know that thou art a teacher come from God - We, all the members of the grand Sanhedrin, and all the rulers of the people, who have paid proper attention to thy doctrine and miracles. We are all convinced of this, though we are not all candid enough to own it. It is possible, however, that οιδαμεν, we know, signifies no more than, it is known, it is generally acknowledged and allowed, that thou art a teacher come from God. <div eID="gen41519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41520" type="x-p"/> No man can do these miracles - It is on the evidence of thy miracles that I ground my opinion of thee. No man can do what thou dost, unless the omnipotence of God be with him.
entries.894bd28fe5a3602dfdf4811557c00b0156587065: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen41520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41521" type="x-p"/> Jesus answered - Not in the language of compliment: - he saw the state of Nicodemus's soul, and he immediately addressed himself to him on a subject the most interesting and important. But what connection is there between our Lord's reply, and the address of Nicodemus? Probably our Lord saw that the object of his visit was to inquire about the Messiah's kingdom; and in reference to this he immediately says, Except a man be born again, etc. <div eID="gen41521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41522" type="x-p"/> The repetition of amen, or verily, verily, among the Jewish writers, was considered of equal import with the most solemn oath. <div eID="gen41522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41523" type="x-p"/> Be born again - Or, from above: different to that new birth which the Jews supposed every baptized proselyte enjoyed; for they held that the Gentile, who became a proselyte, was like a child new born. This birth was of water from below: the birth for which Christ contends is ανωθεν, from above - by the agency of the Holy Spirit. Every man must have two births, one from heaven, the other from earth - one of his body, the other of his soul: without the first he cannot see nor enjoy this world, without the last he can not see nor enjoy the kingdom of God. As there is an absolute necessity that a child should be born into the world, that he may see its light, contemplate its glories, and enjoy its good, so there is an absolute necessity that the soul should be brought out of its state of darkness and sin, through the light and power of the grace of Christ, that it may be able to see, ιδειν, or, to discern, the glories and excellencies of the kingdom of Christ here, and be prepared for the enjoyment of the kingdom of glory hereafter. The Jews had some general notion of the new birth; but, like many among Christians, they put the acts of proselytism, baptism, etc., in the place of the Holy Spirit and his influence: they acknowledged that a man must be born again; but they made that new birth to consist in profession, confession, and external washing. See on <reference osisRef="Joh.3.10">Joh 3:10</reference> (note). <div eID="gen41523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41524" type="x-p"/> The new birth which is here spoken of comprehends, not only what is termed justification or pardon, but also sanctification or holiness. Sin must be pardoned, and the impurity of the heart washed away, before any soul can possibly enter into the kingdom of God. As this new birth implies the renewing of the whole soul in righteousness and true holiness, it is not a matter that may be dispensed with: heaven is a place of holiness, and nothing but what is like itself can ever enter into it.
entries.5935c289c1119247505b3ef7be5945c60c2fe316: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen41524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41525" type="x-p"/> How can a man be born when he is old? - It is probable that Nicodemus was pretty far advanced in age at this time; and from his answer we may plainly perceive that, like the rest of the Jews, and like multitudes of Christians, he rested in the letter, without paying proper attention to the spirit: the shadow, without the thing signified, had hitherto satisfied him. Our Lord knew him to be in this state, and this was the cause of his pointed address to him.
entries.b4ec3f0b9bd7312f1df9c85dbb10405ea4a37252: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen41525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41526" type="x-p"/> Of water and of the Spirit - To the baptism of water a man was admitted when he became a proselyte to the Jewish religion; and, in this baptism, he promised in the most solemn manner to renounce idolatry, to take the God of Israel for his God, and to have his life conformed to the precepts of the Divine law. But the water which was used on the occasion was only an emblem of the Holy Spirit. The soul was considered as in a state of defilement, because of past sin: now, as by that water the body was washed, cleansed, and refreshed, so, by the influences of the Holy Spirit, the soul was to be purified from its defilement, and strengthened to walk in the way of truth and holiness. <div eID="gen41526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41527" type="x-p"/> When John came baptizing with water, he gave the Jews the plainest intimations that this would not suffice; that it was only typical of that baptism of the Holy Ghost, under the similitude of fire, which they must all receive from Jesus Christ: see <reference osisRef="Mat.3.11">Mat 3:11</reference>. Therefore, our Lord asserts that a man must be born of water and the Spirit, i.e. of the Holy Ghost, which, represented under the similitude of water, cleanses, refreshes, and purifies the soul. Reader, hast thou never had any other baptism than that of water? If thou hast not had any other, take Jesus Christ's word for it, thou canst not, in thy present state, enter into the kingdom of God. I would not say to thee merely, read what it is to be born of the Spirit: but pray, O pray to God incessantly, till he give thee to feel what is implied in it! Remember, it is Jesus only who baptizes with the Holy Ghost: see <reference osisRef="Joh.1.33">Joh 1:33</reference>. He who receives not this baptism has neither right nor title to the kingdom of God; nor can he with any propriety be termed a Christian, because that which essentially distinguished the Christian dispensation from that of the Jews was, that its author baptized all his followers with the Holy Ghost. <div eID="gen41527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41528" type="x-p"/> Though baptism by water, into the Christian faith, was necessary to every Jew and Gentile that entered into the kingdom of the Messiah, it is not necessary that by water and the Spirit (in this place) we should understand two different things: it is probably only an elliptical form of speech, for the Holy Spirit under the similitude of water; as, in <reference osisRef="Mat.3.3">Mat 3:3</reference>, the Holy Ghost and fire, do not mean two things, but one, viz. the Holy Ghost under the similitude of fire - pervading every part, refining and purifying the whole.
entries.2f0bc1f44bb484bc6ea1675e6781dbe1c02bc7a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen41528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41529" type="x-p"/> That which is born of the flesh is flesh - This is the answer to the objection made by Nicodemus in <reference osisRef="Joh.3.4">Joh 3:4</reference>. Can a man enter the second time into his mother's womb and be born? Our Lord here intimates that, were even this possible, it would not answer the end; for the plant will ever be of the nature of the seed that produces it - like will beget its like. The kingdom of God is spiritual and holy; and that which is born of the Spirit resembles the Spirit; for as he is who begat, so is he who is begotten of him. Therefore, the spiritual regeneration is essentially necessary, to prepare the soul for a holy and spiritual kingdom.
entries.5be12c2cf04b21fc8df1406088770510419ff57a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen41529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41530" type="x-p"/> The wind bloweth - Though the manner in which this new birth is effected by the Divine Spirit, be incomprehensible to us, yet we must not, on this ground, suppose it to be impossible. The wind blows in a variety of directions - we hear its sound, perceive its operation in the motion of the trees, etc., and feel it on ourselves - but we cannot discern the air itself; we only know that it exists by the effects which it produces: so is every one who is born of the Spirit: the effects are as discernible and as sensible as those of the wind; but itself we cannot see. But he who is born of God knows that he is thus born: the Spirit itself, the grand agent in this new birth, beareth witness with his spirit, that he is born of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.16">Rom 8:16</reference>; for, he that believeth hath the witness in himself, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.13">1Jn 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.10">1Jn 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal 4:6</reference>. And so does this Spirit work in and by him that others, though they see not the principle, can easily discern the change produced; for whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.4">1Jn 5:4</reference>.
entries.685163aa30b3ee408a71b96e59e359f2d98dd43c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen41530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41531" type="x-p"/> How can these things be? - Our Lord had very plainly told him how these things could be, and illustrated the new birth by one of the most proper similes that could be chosen; but so intent was this great man an making every thing submit to the testimony of his senses that he appears unwilling to believe any thing, unless he can comprehend it. This is the case with many - they profess to believe because they comprehend; but they are impostors who speak thus: there is not a man in the universe that can fully comprehend one operation, either of God or his instrument nature; and yet they must believe, and do believe, though they never did nor ever can fully comprehend, or account for, the objects of their faith.
