entries.f43d80a645073a6898afc55e82f882ae7c2ca325: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.17" sID="gen103972" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17. </hi><hi type="italic">For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world.</hi> It is a confirmation of the preceding statement; for it was not in vain that God sent his own Son to us. He came not to destroy; and therefore it follows, that it is the peculiar office of the Son of God, that <hi type="italic">all who believe</hi> may obtain salvation by him. There is now no reason why any man should be in a state of hesitation, or of distressing anxiety, as to the manner in which he may escape death, when we believe that it was the purpose of God that Christ should deliver us from it. The word <hi type="italic">world</hi> is again repeated, that no man may think himself wholly excluded, if he only keep the road of faith.<div eID="gen103973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103974" type="x-p"/>The word <hi type="italic">judge</hi> (<foreign xml:lang="el">πρίνω</foreign>) is here put for condemn, as in many other passages. When he declares that <hi type="italic">he did not come to condemn the world</hi>, he thus points out the actual design of his coming; for what need was there that Christ should come to destroy us who were utterly ruined? We ought not, therefore, to look at any thing else in Christ, than that God, out of his boundless goodness chose to extend his aid for saving us who were lost; and whenever our sins press us — whenever Satan would drive us to despair — we ought to hold out this shield, that God is unwilling that we should be overwhelmed with everlasting destruction, because he has appointed his Son to be the salvation of the <hi type="italic">world</hi><div eID="gen103974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103975" type="x-p"/>When Christ says, in other passages, that <hi type="italic">he is come to judgment</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.9.39">John 9:39</reference>;) when he is called <hi type="italic">a stone of offense</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.7">1 Peter 2:7</reference>;) when he is said to be <hi type="italic">set for the destruction of many</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.34">Luke 2:34</reference>:) this may be regarded as accidental, or as arising from a different cause; for they who reject the grace offered in him deserve to find him the Judge and Avenger of contempt so unworthy and base. A striking instance of this may be seen in the Gospel; for though it is strictly<div eID="gen103975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103976" type="x-p"/>the power of God for salvation to every one who believeth, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.16">Romans 1:16</reference>,)<div eID="gen103976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103977" type="x-p"/>the ingratitude of many causes it to become to them death. Both have been well expressed by Paul, when he boasts of<div eID="gen103977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103978" type="x-p"/>having vengeance at hand, by which he will punish all the adversaries of his doctrine after that the obedience of the godly shall have been fulfilled, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.6">2 Corinthians 10:6</reference>)<div eID="gen103978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103979" type="x-p"/>The meaning amounts to this, that the Gospel is especially, and in the first instance, appointed for believers, that it may be salvation to them; but that afterwards believers will not escape unpunished who, despising the grace of Christ, chose to have him as the Author of death rather than of life.<div eID="gen103979" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103972" osisID="John.3.17" type="section"/>
entries.c06f01a666a20bfb3f7c476b8a5ad31f4919b085:
18. He who believeth in him is not condemned. When he so frequently and so earnestly repeats, that all believers are beyond danger of death, we may infer from it the great necessity of firm and assured confidence, that the conscience may not be kept perpetually in a state of trembling and alarm. He again declares that, when we have believed, there is no remaining condemnation, which he will afterwards explain more fully in the Fifth Chapter. The present tense — is not condemned — is here used instead of the future tense — shall not be condemned — according to the custom of the Hebrew language; for he means that believers are safe from the fear of condemnation.
But he who believeth not is condemned already This means that there is no other remedy by which any human being can escape death; or, in other words, that for all who reject the life given to them in Christ, there remains nothing but death, since life consists in nothing else than in faith. The past tense of the verb, is condemned already, (ἤδη κέκριται,) was used by him emphatically, (ἐμφατικῶς,) to express more strongly that all unbelievers are utterly ruined. But it ought to be observed that Christ speaks especially of those whose wickedness shall be displayed in open contempt of the Gospel. For though it is true that there never was any other remedy for escaping death than that men should betake themselves to Christ, yet as Christ here speaks of the preaching of the Gospel, which was to be spread throughout the whole world, he directs his discourse against those who deliberately and maliciously extinguish the light which God had kindled.
John 3:19-21
19. And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world; and men loved darkness rather than light; for their works were evil. 20. For whosoever doeth what is evil hateth the light, and cometh not to the light, that his works may not be discovered. 21. But he who doeth truth cometh to the light, that his works may be made manifest, that they are done in God.
“Faites selon Dieu;” — “done according to God.”
entries.25419ca10448cde61f655f6bb6c7d1332043ca38: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.19" sID="gen103988" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">And this is the condemnation</hi> He meets the murmurs and complaints, by which wicked men are wont to censure — what they imagine to be the excessive rigour of God, when he acts towards them with greater severity than they expected. All think it harsh that they who do not believe in Christ should be devoted to destruction. That no man may ascribe his <hi type="italic">condemnation</hi> to Christ, he shows that every man ought to impute the blame to himself. The reason is, that unbelief is a testimony of a bad conscience; and hence it is evident that it is their own wickedness which hinders unbelievers from approaching to Christ. Some think that he points out here nothing more than the mark of <hi type="italic">condemnation</hi>; but, the design of Christ is, to restrain the wickedness of men, that they may not, according to their custom, dispute or argue with God, as if he treated them unjustly, when he punishes unbelief with eternal death. He shows that such a <hi type="italic">condemnation</hi> is just, and is not liable to any reproaches, not only because those men act wickedly, who prefer<hi type="italic"> darkness</hi> to<hi type="italic"> light</hi>, and refuse the <hi type="italic">light </hi>which is freely offered to them, but because that <hi type="italic">hatred of the light </hi>arises only from a mind that is wicked and conscious of its guilt. A beautiful appearance and lustre of holiness may indeed be found in many, who, after all, oppose the Gospel; but, though they appear to be holier than the angels, there is no room to doubt that they are hypocrites, who reject the doctrine of Christ for no other reason than because they love their lurking-places by which their baseness may be concealed. Since, therefore, hypocrisy alone renders men hateful to God, all are held convicted, because were it not that, blinded by pride, they delight in their crimes, they would readily and willingly receive the doctrine of the Gospel.<div eID="gen103989" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103988" osisID="John.3.19" type="section"/>
entries.1267a7d93527a2ebff85db9cb38b4daba8586315: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.20" sID="gen103990" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi><hi type="italic"> For whosoever doeth what is evil.</hi> The meaning is, that <hi type="italic">the light</hi> is hateful to them for no other reason than because they are wicked and desire to conceal their sins, as far as lies in their power. Hence it follows that, by rejecting the remedy, they may be said purposely to cherish the ground of their condemnation. We are greatly mistaken, therefore, if we suppose that they who are enraged against the Gospel are actuated by godly zeal, when, on the contrary, they abhor and shun the light, that they may more freely flatter themselves in <hi type="italic">darkness</hi><div eID="gen103991" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103990" osisID="John.3.20" type="section"/>
entries.f265540ae8bfc23c318848b4bed917a80619df18:
21. But he who doeth truth This appears to be an improper and absurd statement, unless you choose to admit that some are upright and true, before they have been renewed by the Spirit of God, which does not at all agree with the uniform doctrine of Scripture; for we know that faith is the root from which the fruits of good works spring. To solve this difficulty, Augustine says, that to do truth means “to acknowledge that we are miserable and destitute of all power of doing good;” and, certainly, it is a true preparation for faith, when a conviction of our poverty compels us to flee to the grace of God. But all this is widely removed from Christ’s meaning, for he intended simply to say that those who act sincerely desire nothing more earnestly than light, that their works may be tried; because, when such a trial has been made, it becomes more evident that, in the sight of God, they speak the truth and are free from all deceit. Now it would be inconclusive reasoning, were we to infer from this, that men have a good conscience before they have faith; for Christ does not say that the elect believe, so as to deserve the praise of good works, but only what unbelievers would do, if they had not a bad conscience.
Christ employed the word truth, because, when we are deceived by the outward lustre of works, we do not consider what is concealed within. Accordingly, he says, that men who are upright and free from hypocrisy willingly go into the presence of God, who alone is the competent Judge of our works. For those works are said to be done in God or according to God, which are approved by Him, and which are good according to His rule. Hence let us learn that we must not judge of works in any other way than by bringing them to the light of the Gospel, because our reason is wholly blind.
John 3:22-28
22. After these things came Jesus, and his disciples, into the land of Judea, and there he remained with them and baptized. 23. And John also was baptizing in Enon, near Salim; because there were many waters there. They came therefore and were baptized. 24. For John was not yet cast into prison. 25. A question then arose between the disciples of John and the Jews about purifying. 26. And they came to John, and said to him, Rabbi, he who was with thee beyond Jordan, to whom thou gavest testimony, lo, he baptizeth, and all men come to him. 27. John answered and said, A man cannot receive any thing, unless it be given to him from heaven. 28. Yourselves are witnesses to me, that I said, I am not Christ, but was sent before him.
entries.f32667a859394148b18d9ff0370d1a82ed00000d: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.22" sID="gen103999" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> <hi type="italic">After these things came Jesus.</hi> It is probable that Christ, when the feast was past, came into that part of Judea which was in the vicinity of the town <hi type="italic">Enon</hi>, which was situated in the tribe of Manasseh. The Evangelist says that <hi type="italic">there were many waters there</hi>, and these were not so abundant in Judea. Now geographers tell us, that these two towns, <hi type="italic">Enon </hi>and <hi type="italic">Salim</hi>, were not far from the confluence of the river Jordan and the brook Jabbok; and they add that Scythopolis was near them. From these words, we may infer that John and Christ administered baptism by plunging the whole body beneath the water; though we ought not to give ourselves any great uneasiness about the outward rite, provided that it agree with the spiritual truth, and with the Lord’s appointment and rule. So far as we are able to conjecture, the; vicinity of those places caused various reports to be circulated, and many discussions to arise, about the Law, about the worship of God, and about the condition of the Church, in consequence of two persons who administered baptism having arisen at the same time. For when the Evangelist says that <hi type="italic">Christ baptized</hi>, I refer this to the commencement of his ministry; namely, that he then began to exercise publicly the office which was appointed to him by the Father. And though Christ did this by his disciples, yet he is here named as the Author of the baptism, without mentioning his ministers, who did nothing but in his name and by his command. On this subject, we shall have something more to say in the beginning of the next Chapter.<div eID="gen104000" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103999" osisID="John.3.22" type="section"/>
entries.286beee9d9189e7e41252a12933a69d99e897b62: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.25" sID="gen104001" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi><hi type="italic"> A question then arose.</hi> Not without a good reason does the Evangelist relate that <hi type="italic">a question arose from the disciples of John</hi>; for just in proportion as they were ill-informed about doctrine, they are so much the more eager to enter into debate, as ignorance is always bold and presumptuous. If others had attacked them, they might have been excused; but when they themselves, though unfit to maintain the contest, voluntarily provoke the Jews, it is a rash and foolish proceeding. Now the words mean, that “the<hi type="italic"> question </hi>was raised by them;” and not only were they to blame for taking up a matter which they did not understand, and speaking about it rashly and beyond the measure of their knowledge; but another fault — not less than the former — was, that they did not so much intend to maintain the lawfulness of Baptism as to defend the cause of their master, that his authority might remain unimpaired. In both respects, they deserved reproof, because, not understanding what was the real nature of Baptism, they expose the holy ordinance of God to ridicule, and because, by sinful ambition, they undertake to defend the cause of their master against Christ.<div eID="gen104002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104003" type="x-p"/>It is evident, therefore, that they were astonished and confounded by a single word, when it was represented to them that <hi type="italic">Christ also was baptizing</hi>; for while their attention was directed to the person of a man, and to outward appearance, <note n="64"> <div sID="gen104004" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et apparence exterieure</foreign>.”<div eID="gen104004" type="x-p"/> </note> they gave themselves less concern about the doctrine. We are taught, by their example, into what mistakes those men fall who are actuated by a sinful desire to please men rather than by a zeal for God; and we are likewise reminded that the single object which we ought to have in view and to promote by all means is, that Christ alone may have the pre-eminence.<div eID="gen104003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104005" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">About purifying</hi> The <hi type="italic">question</hi> was <hi type="italic">about purifying</hi>; for the Jews had various baptisms and washings <note n="65"> <div sID="gen104006" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De baptesmes et lavemens</foreign>.”<div eID="gen104006" type="x-p"/> </note> enjoined by the Law; and not satisfied with those which God had appointed, <note n="66"> <div sID="gen104007" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que Dieu avoit instituez</foreign>.”<div eID="gen104007" type="x-p"/> </note> they carefully observed many others which had been handed down from their ancestors. When they find that, in addition to so great a number and variety of <hi type="italic">purifyings</hi>, a new method of <hi type="italic">purifying </hi>is introduced by Christ and by John, they look upon it as absurd.<div eID="gen104005" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104001" osisID="John.3.25" type="section"/>
entries.7eb85dfac854c265d757f8675dd98bb7c88adb68: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.26" sID="gen104008" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">To whom thou gavest testimony.</hi> By this argument they endeavor either to make Christ inferior to John, or to show that John, by doing him honor, had laid him under obligations; for they reckon that John conferred a favor on Christ by adorning him with such honorable titles. As if it had not been the duty of John to make such a proclamation, or rather, as if it had not been John’s highest dignity to be the herald of the Son of God. Nothing could have been more unreasonable than to make Christ inferior to John, because his testimony was highly favorable; for we know what John’s testimony was. The expression which they use — <hi type="italic">all men come to Christ</hi> — is the language of envious persons, <note n="67"> <div sID="gen104010" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est une parole de gens envieux</foreign>.”<div eID="gen104010" type="x-p"/> </note> and proceeds from sinful ambition; for they are afraid that the crowd will immediately forsake their master.<div eID="gen104009" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104008" osisID="John.3.26" type="section"/>
entries.4095a276bf4d65f940336063c150b9412996f33f: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.27" sID="gen104011" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi><hi type="italic"> A man cannot receive any thing.</hi> Some refer these words to Christ, as if John accused the disciples of wicked presumption in opposition to God, by endeavoring to deprive Christ of what the Father had given to him. They suppose the meaning to be this: “That within so short a time he has risen to so great honor, is the work of God; and therefore it is in vain for you to attempt to degrade him whom God with his own hand has raised on high.” Others think that it is an exclamation into which he indignantly breaks forth, because his disciples had hitherto made so little progress. And certainly it was excessively absurd that they should still endeavor to reduce to the rank of ordinary men him who, they had so often heard, was the Christ, that he might not rise above his own servants; and, therefore, John might justly have said that it is useless to spend time in instructing men, because they are dull and stupid, until they are renewed in mind.<div eID="gen104012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104013" type="x-p"/>But I rather agree with the opinion of those who explain it as applying to John, as asserting that it is not in his power, or in theirs, to make him great, because the measure of us all is to be what God intended us to be. For if even the Son of God <hi type="italic">took not that honour to himself</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.5.4">Hebrews 5:4</reference>,) what man of the ordinary rank would venture to desire more than what the Lord has given him? This single thought, if it were duly impressed on the minds of us all, would be abundantly sufficient for restraining ambition; and were ambition corrected and destroyed, the plague of contentions would likewise be removed. How comes it then, that every man exalts himself more than is proper, but because we do not depend on the Lord, so as to be satisfied with the rank which he assigns to us?<div eID="gen104013" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104011" osisID="John.3.27" type="section"/>
entries.4cad3bd049995affd5ab466e96d159f8b332d315:
28. You are witnesses to me. John expostulates with his disciples that they did not give credit to his statements. He had often warned them that he was not the Christ; and, therefore, it only remained that he should be a servant and subject to the Son of God along with others. And this passage is worthy of notice; for, by affirming that he is not the Christ, he reserves nothing for himself but to be subject to the head, and to serve in the Church as one of the rest, and not to be so highly exalted as to obscure the honor of the Head. He says that he was sent before, to prepare the way for Christ, as kings are wont to have heralds or forerunners.
John 3:29-34
29. He who hath the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who standeth, and heareth him, rejoiceth exceedingly on account of the bridegroom’s voice. This my joy, therefore, is fulfilled. 30. He must increase, but I must decrease. 31. He who cometh from above is above all; he who is from the earth is of the earth, and speaketh
“Et parle de la terre, ou, comme issu de terre;” — “and speaketh of the earthy or, as having proceeded from the earth.”
of the earth: he who cometh from heaven is above all. 32. And what he hath seen and heard, this he testifieth, and no man receiveth his testimony. 33. But he who receiveth his testimony hath sealed that God is true. 34. For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God, for God giveth not the Spirit by measure.
entries.2f2d9797949280ebdeca427847510911e7f6dad9: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.29" sID="gen104021" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi><hi type="italic"> He who hath the bride.</hi> By this comparison, he confirms more fully the statement, that it is Christ alone who is excluded from the ordinary rank of men. For as he who marries a wife does not call and invite his friends to the marriage, in order to prostitute the bride to them, or, by giving up his own rights, to allow them to partake with him of the nuptial bed, but rather that the marriage, being honored by them, may be rendered more sacred; so Christ does not call his ministers to the office of teaching, in order that, by conquering the Church, they may claim dominion over it, but that he may make use of their faithful labors for associating them with himself. It is a great and lofty distinction, that men are appointed over the Church, to represent the person of the Son of God. They are, therefore, like <hi type="italic">the friends</hi> whom<hi type="italic"> the bridegroom</hi> brings with him, that they may accompany him in celebrating the marriage; but we must attend to the distinction, that ministers, being mindful of their rank, may not appropriate to themselves what belongs exclusively to <hi type="italic">the bridegroom</hi> The whole amounts to this, that all the eminence which teachers may possess among themselves ought not to hinder Christ from ruling alone in his Church, or from governing it alone by his word.<div eID="gen104022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104023" type="x-p"/>This comparison frequently occurs in Scripture, when the Lord intends to express the sacred bond of adoption, by which he binds us to himself. For as he offers himself to be truly enjoyed by us, that he may be ours, so he justly claims from us that mutual fidelity and love which the wife owes to her husband. This marriage is entirely fulfilled in Christ, <hi type="italic">whose flesh and bones </hi>we are, as Paul informs us, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.30">Ephesians 5:30</reference>.) The chastity demanded by him consists chiefly in the obedience of the Gospel, that we may not suffer ourselves to be led aside from its pure simplicity, as the same Apostle teaches us, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.11.2 Bible:2Cor.11.3">2 Corinthians 11:2, 3</reference>.) We must, therefore, be subject to Christ alone, he must be our only Head, we must not turn aside a hair’s-breadth from the simple doctrine of the Gospel, he alone must have the highest glory, that he may retain the right and authority of being a bridegroom to us.<div eID="gen104023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104024" type="x-p"/>But what are ministers to do? Certainly, the Son of God calls them, that they may perform their duty to him in conducting the sacred marriage; and, therefore, their duty is, to take care, in every way, that the <hi type="italic">spouse</hi> — who is committed to their charge — may be presented by them <hi type="italic">as a chaste virgin </hi>to her husband; which Paul, in the passage already quoted, boasts of having done. But they who draw the Church to themselves rather than to Christ are guilty of basely violating the marriage which they ought to have honored. And the greater the honor which Christ confers on us, by making us the guardians of his spouse, so much the more heinous is our want of fidelity, if we do not endeavor to maintain and defend his right.<div eID="gen104024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104025" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">This my joy therefore is fulfilled.</hi> He means that he has obtained the fulfillment of all his desires, and that he has nothing further to wish, when he sees Christ reigning, and men listening to him as he deserves. Whoever shall have such affections that, laying aside all regard to himself, he shall extol Christ and be satisfied with seeing Christ honored, will be faithful and successful in ruling the Church; but, whoever shall swerve from that end in the slightest degree will be a base adulterer, and will do nothing else than corrupt the spouse of Christ.<div eID="gen104025" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104021" osisID="John.3.29" type="section"/>
entries.d1909e7769be99b7c6a7f901000b73e2b5d10011: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.30" sID="gen104026" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">He must increase.</hi> John the Baptist proceeds farther; for, having formerly been raised by the Lord to the highest dignity, he shows that this was only for a time, but now that <hi type="italic">the Sun of Righteousness</hi>,<hi type="italic"> </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.4.2">Malachi 4:2</reference>) has arisen, he must give way; and, therefore, he not only scatters and drives away the empty fumes of honor which had been rashly and ignorantly heaped upon him by men, but also is exceedingly careful that the true and lawful honor which the Lord had bestowed on him may not obscure the glory of Christ. Accordingly, he tells us that the reason why he had been hitherto accounted a great Prophet was, that for a time only he was placed in so lofty a station, until Christ came, to whom he must surrender his office. In the meantime, he declares that he will most willingly endure to be reduced to nothing, provided that Christ occupy and fill the whole world with his rays; and this zeal of John all pastors of the Church ought to imitate by stooping with the head and shoulders to elevate Christ.<div eID="gen104027" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104026" osisID="John.3.30" type="section"/>
entries.53436b9c78da4ea1a06b1e4b333cd8ead0a391f4: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.31" sID="gen104028" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31.</hi> <hi type="italic">He who cometh from above.</hi> By another comparison he shows how widely Christ differs from all the rest, and how far he is above them; for he compares him to a king or distinguished general, who, speaking from his lofty seat, ought to be heard with reverence for his authority, but shows that it is enough for himself to speak from the lowest footstool of Christ. <note n="69"> <div sID="gen104030" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Au marchepied de Christ</foreign>.”<div eID="gen104030" type="x-p"/> </note> In the second clause the old Latin translation has only once the words, <hi type="italic">is of the earth;</hi> but the Greek manuscripts agree in repeating the words twice. I suspect that ignorant men considered the repetition to be superfluous, and therefore erased it; but the meaning is: <hi type="italic">he who is of earth </hi>gives evidence of his descent, and remains in an earthly rank according to the condition of his nature. He maintains that it is peculiar to Christ alone to speak <hi type="italic">from above</hi>, because <hi type="italic">he came from heaven</hi><div eID="gen104029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104031" type="x-p"/>But it may be asked, Did not John also <hi type="italic">come from heaven</hi>, as to his calling and office, and was it not therefore the duty of men to hear the Lord speaking by his mouth? For he appears to do injustice to the heavenly doctrine which he delivers. I reply, this was not said absolutely, but by comparison. If ministers be separately considered, they speak as <hi type="italic">from heaven</hi>, with the highest authority, what God commanded them; but, as soon as they begin to be contrasted with Christ, they must no longer be anything. Thus the Apostle, comparing the Law with the Gospel, says,<div eID="gen104031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104032" type="x-p"/>Since they escaped not who despised him that spoke on earth, beware lest you despise him who is from heaven,<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.25">Hebrews 12:25</reference>.)<div eID="gen104032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104033" type="x-p"/>Christ, therefore, wishes to be acknowledged in his ministers, but in such a manner that he may remain the only Lord, and that they may be satisfied with the rank of servants; but especially when a comparison is made, he wishes to be so distinguished that he alone may be exalted.<div eID="gen104033" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104028" osisID="John.3.31" type="section"/>
entries.86d1f7730cc591a0e693c4610aafc71eb3539661: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.32" sID="gen104034" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32.</hi><hi type="italic"> And what he hath seen and heard.</hi> John proceeds in the discharge of his office; for, in order to procure disciples for Christ, he commends Christ’s doctrine as certain, because he utters nothing but what he has received from the Father. <hi type="italic">Seeing </hi>and <hi type="italic">hearing </hi>are contrasted with doubtful opinions, unfounded rumors, and every kind of falsehoods; for he means that Christ teaches nothing but what has been fully ascertained. But some one will say that little credit is due to him who has nothing but <hi type="italic">what he has heard.</hi> I reply, this word denotes that Christ has been taught by the Father, so that he brings forward nothing but what is divine, or, in other words, what has been revealed to him by God.<div eID="gen104035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104036" type="x-p"/>Now this belongs to the whole person of Christ, so far as the Father sent him into the world as His ambassador and interpreter. He afterwards charges the world with ingratitude, in basely and wickedly rejecting such an undoubted and faithful interpreter of God. In this way he meets the offense which might cause many to turn aside from the faith, and might hinder or retard the progress of many; for, as we are accustomed to depend too much on the judgment of the world, a considerable number of persons judge of the Gospel by the contempt of the world, or at least, where they see it everywhere rejected, they are prejudiced by that event, and are rendered more unwilling and more slow to believe. And, therefore, whenever we see such obstinacy in the world, let this admonition hold us in constant obedience to the Gospel, that it is truth which came from God. When he says that NO-MAN<hi type="italic">, receiveth his testimony,</hi> he means that there are very few and almost no believers, when compared with the vast crowd of unbelievers.<div eID="gen104036" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104034" osisID="John.3.32" type="section"/>
entries.8800aeced74442d16e753582d457aab13eb6fbbd: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.33" sID="gen104037" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">33.</hi><hi type="italic"> But he who receiveth his testimony.</hi> Here he exhorts and encourages the godly to embrace boldly the doctrine of the Gospel, as if he had said that there was no reason why they should be ashamed or uneasy on account of their small number, since they have God as the Author of their faith, who alone abundantly supplies to us the place of all the rest. And, therefore, though the whole world should refuse or withhold faith in the Gospel, this ought not to prevent good men from giving their assent to God. They have something on which they may safely rest, when they know that to believe the Gospel is nothing else than to assent to the truths which God has revealed. Meanwhile, we learn that it is peculiar to faith to rely on God, and to be confirmed by his words; for there can be no assent, unless God have, first of all, come forward and spoken. By this doctrine faith is not only distinguished from all human inventions, but likewise from doubtful and wavering opinions; for it must correspond to the truth of God, which is free from all doubt, and therefore, as God cannot lie, it would be absurd that faith should waver. Fortified by this defense, whatever contrivances Satan may employ in his attempts to disturb and shake us, we shall always remain victorious.<div eID="gen104038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen104039" type="x-p"/>Hence, too, we are reminded how acceptable and precious a sacrifice in the sight of God faith is. As nothing is more dear to him than his truth, so we cannot render to him more acceptable worship than when we acknowledge by our faith that He is true, for then we ascribe that honor which truly belongs to him. On the other hand, we cannot offer to him a greater insult than not to believe the Gospel; for he cannot be deprived of his truth without taking away all his glory and majesty. His truth is in some sort closely linked with the Gospel, and it is his will that there it should be recognized. Unbelievers, therefore, as far as lies in their power, leave to God nothing whatever; not that their wickedness overthrows the faithfulness of God, but because they do not hesitate to charge God with falsehood. If we are not harder than stones, this lofty title by which faith is adorned ought to kindle in our minds the most ardent love of it; for how great is the honor which God confers on poor worthless men, when they, who by nature are nothing else than falsehood and vanity, are thought worthy of attesting by their signature the sacred truth of God?<div eID="gen104039" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104037" osisID="John.3.33" type="section"/>
entries.3fb9385b8bbbb043abbbf648cb90120233e556ff:
34. For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God. He confirms the preceding statement, for he shows that we have actually to do with God, when we receive the doctrine of Christ; because Christ proceeded from none else than from the Heavenly Father. It is, therefore, God alone who speaks to us by him; and, indeed, we do not assign to the doctrine of Christ all that it deserves, unless we acknowledge it to be divine.
For God giveth not the Spirit by measure. This passage is explained in two ways. Some extend it to the ordinary dispensation in this manner: that God, who is the inexhaustible fountain of all benefits, does not in the least degree diminish his resources, when he largely and plentifully bestows his gifts on men. They who draw from any vessel what they give to others come at last to the bottom; but there is no danger that any thing of this sort can happen with God, nor will the abundance of his gifts ever be so large that he cannot go beyond it, whenever he shall be pleased to make a new exercise of liberality. This exposition appears to have some plausibility, for the sentence is indefinite; that is, it does not expressly point out any person.
“C’est a dire, ne determine point certaine personne.”
But I am more disposed to follow Augustine, who explains that it was said concerning Christ. Nor is there any force in the objection, that no express mention is made of Christ in this clause, since all ambiguity is removed by the next clause, in which that which might seem to have been said indiscriminately about many is limited to Christ. For these words were unquestionably added for the sake of explanation, that the Father hath given all things into the hand of his Son, because he loveth him, and ought therefore to be read as placed in immediate connection. The verb in the present tense — giveth — denotes, as it were, a continued act; for though Christ was all at once endued with the Spirit in the highest perfection, yet, as he continually flows, as it were, from a source, and is widely diffused, there is no impropriety in saying that Christ now receives him from the Father. But if any one choose to interpret it more simply, it is no unusual thing that there should be a change of tenses in such verbs, and that giveth should be put for hath given
“Et que Donne soit mis pour et donne.”
The meaning is now plain, that the Spirit was not given to Christ by measure, as if the power of grace which he possesses were in any way limited; as Paul teaches that
to every one is given according to the measure of the gift, (Ephesians 4:7,)
so that there is no one who alone has full abundance. For while this is the mutual bond of brotherly intercourse between us, that no man separately considered has every thing that he needs, but all require the aid of each other, Christ differs from us in this respect, that the Father has poured out upon him an unlimited abundance of his Spirit. And, certainly, it is proper that the Spirit should dwell without measure in him, that we may all draw out of his fullness, as we have seen in the first chapter. And to this relates what immediately follows, that the Father hath given all things into his hand; for by these words John the Baptist not only declares the excellence of Christ, but, at the same time, points out the end and use of the riches with which he is endued; namely, that Christ, having been appointed by the Father to be the administrator, he distributes to every one as he chooses, and as he finds to be necessary; as Paul explains more fully in the fourth chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians, which I lately quoted. Although God enriches his own people in a variety of ways, this is peculiar to Christ alone, that he has all things in his hand
John 3:35-36
35. The Father loveth the Son, and hath given all things into his hand. 36. He who believeth in the Son hath eternal life; but he who believeth not in the Son
“Qui ne croit point au Fils, ou, qui desobeit au Fils;” — “who believeth not in the Son, or, who disobeyeth the Son.”
shall not see life, but the wrath of God abideth on him.
entries.6696f8014a0a9f1deacf07a93463c22224754f31: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.35" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.3.35" sID="gen104054" type="section"/> <div sID="gen104055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">35.</hi> <hi type="italic">The Father loveth the Son.</hi> But what is the meaning of this reason? Does he regard all others with hatred? The answer is easy, that he does not speak of the common love with which God regards men whom he has created, or his other works, but of that peculiar love which, beginning with the Son, flows from him to all the creatures. For that love with which, embracing the Son, he embraces us also in him, leads him to communicate all his benefits to us by his hand.<div eID="gen104055" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.3.35" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen104054" osisID="John.3.35" type="section"/>
entries.2c4d7b4ca8cfd8597ee36774fa6f397de3e5f519:
36. He who believeth in the Son. This was added, not only to inform us that we ought to ask all good things from Christ, but likewise to make us, acquainted with the manner in which they are enjoyed. He shows that enjoyment consists in faith; and not without reason, since by means of it we possess Christ, who brings along with him both righteousness and life, which is the fruit of righteousness. When faith in Christ is declared to be the cause of life, we learn from it that life is to be found in Christ alone, and that in no other way do we become partakers of it than by the grace of Christ himself. But all are not agreed as to the way in which the life of Christ comes to us. Some understand it thus: “as by believing we receive the Spirit, who regenerates us in order to justification, by that very regeneration we obtain salvation.” For my own part, though I acknowledge it to be true, that we are renewed by faith, so that the Spirit of Christ governs us, yet I say that we ought first to take into consideration the free forgiveness of sins, through which we are accepted by God. Again, I say that on this all our confidence of salvation is founded, and in this it consists; because justification before God cannot be reckoned to us in any other way than when he does not impute to us our sins.
But he who believeth not in the Son. As he held out life in Christ, by the sweetness of which he might allure us, so now he adjudges to eternal death all who do not believe in Christ. And, in this way, he magnifies the kindness of God, when he warns us, that there is no other way of escaping death, unless Christ deliver us; for this sentence depends on the fact, that we are all accursed in Adam. Now if it be the office of Christ to save what was lost, they who reject the salvation offered in him are justly suffered to remain in death. We have just now said that this belongs peculiarly to those who reject the gospel which has been revealed to them; for though all mankind are involved in the same destruction, yet a heavier and double vengeance awaits those who refuse to have the Son of God as their deliverer. And, indeed, it cannot be doubted that the Baptist, when he denounced death against unbelievers, intended to excite us, by the dread of it, to the exercise of faith in Christ. It is also manifest; that all the righteousness which the world thinks that it has out of Christ is condemned and reduced to nothing. Nor is any one enabled to object that it is unjust that those who are otherwise devout and holy should perish, because they do not believe; for it is folly to imagine that there is any holiness in men, unless it have been given to them by Christ.
To see life is here put for “enjoying life.” But to express more clearly that no hope remains for us, unless we are delivered by Christ, he says that the wrath of God abideth on unbelievers. Though I am not dissatisfied with the view given by Augustine, that John the Baptist used the word abideth, in order to inform us that, from the womb we were appointed to death, because we are all born the children of wrath, (Ephesians 2:3.) At least, I willingly admit an allusion of this sort, provided we hold the true and simple meaning to be what I have stated, that death hangs over all unbelievers, and keeps them oppressed and overwhelmed in such a manner that they can never escape. And, indeed, though already the reprobate are naturally condemned, yet by their unbelief they draw down on themselves a new death. And it is for this purpose that the power of binding was given to the ministers of the gospel; for it is a just vengeance on the obstinacy of men, that they who shake off the salutary yoke of God should bind themselves with the chains of death.
CHAPTER 4
John 4:1-9
1. When, therefore, the Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus made and baptized more disciples than John, (2. Though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples,) 3. He left Judea, and departed again into Galilee. 4. And it was necessary that he should pass through Samaria. 5. He came, therefore, into the city of Samaria, which is called Sichar, near a field which Jacob gave to his son Joseph. 6. And Jacob’s well was there; and Jesus, fatigued by the journey, was thus sitting on the well, for it was about the sixth hour. 7. A woman came from Samaria to draw water. Jesus saith to her, Give me to drink. 8. For the disciples had gone into the city to buy food. 9. The Samaritan woman saith to him, How dost thou, who art a Jew, ask drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman? For the Jews hold no intercourse with the Samaritans.

entries.206d8689a1fac4f0c00dadc7e352ff7d5bdb567b:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="3" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. III.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p>THere <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The particle <ns0:hi>there,</ns0:hi> being put in onely to fit our Idiom to the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> where is nothing but the Verb, signifies no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing to prove, that what we read in this Chapter was done at <ns0:hi>Hierusalem</ns0:hi>; it is a dispute amongst some Interpreters, whether he was there or no, it should seem by <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 7. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 50. that <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> his chief Residence was there; he was</ns0:note> was a man of the Pharisees <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">one of the Pharisees, who were a sect (as we have shewed before) which had their name either from an <ns0:hi>He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew</ns0:hi> word, which signifieth to <ns0:hi>explain,</ns0:hi> (because they were expounders of the Law); or from another word, which signifieth to <ns0:hi>divide,</ns0:hi> because they were separate from others: the Opinions have both learned Patrons.</ns0:note>, named Nicodemus <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This mans name in <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> signifies the <ns0:hi>Victory of the People</ns0:hi>:</ns0:note>, a ruler of the Jews <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">he was either the head of a Family among the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> or a Ruler of the Synagogue, or one of the <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim</ns0:hi>; it seem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth most probable he is here called a <ns0:hi>Ruler</ns0:hi> upon the last account, if we consider <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 7.50.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 The same came unto Jesus by night <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He came by night to Christ, not as some (too chari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tably) possibly may think, that he might have the freer and less interrupted Communion and Discourse with him; but either through fear, or possibly shame, (being a Master in <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi>) to be lookt upon as a Scholar going to learn of another.</ns0:note>, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er come from God <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He saluteth him by the Name they usually gave to their <ns0:hi>Teachers,</ns0:hi> (as we shewed in the foregoing Chapter, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 49. and saith, <ns0:hi>we know,</ns0:hi> by which he hinteth to us, that not onely he, but others of the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> also knew that he was a Teacher sent from God in a more extraor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary manner;</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9.16, 33.</ns0:note> no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 10.38.</ns0:note> God be with him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">and he giveth the reason of this their Knowledg, because of those miraculous Operations which he had wrought. God hath his number among all orders and sorts of men; and those that are his, shall come unto Christ<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> there was a weakness in the <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> and Love of this <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi>; (his Station amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> was a great Temptation to him,) but yet there was a truth of both in him, which further discovered it self, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 7.50. and more up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on Christs death, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 19.39. But here ariseth a grea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter question, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> How <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> could conclude that Christ was a teacher sent from God, by his Miracles? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> It is to be observed, that he doth not say in the general, that no man does Signs or Wonders of any kind, unless the Power and Favour of God be with him. But he speaks particu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larly and eminently of those things which Jesus did; they were so great in their nature, so real and solid in their proof, so divine in the manner of performing them by the Empire of his Will; so holy in their end, to confirm a Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine most becoming the Wisdom and other glorious At<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tributes of God, and that were the verification of the Prophecies concerning the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> whose coming was foretold should be with miraculous healing benefits; that there was the greatest assurance, that none without the Omnipotent hand of God could do them; for 'tis clear by the light of Reason and Scripture, that God will not assist by his Almighty Power the Ministers of Satan, to induce those who sincerely search for Truth to believe a Lye. The Magicians indeed performed divers Wonders in <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> but they were outdone by <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> to convince the Specta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tors, that he was sent from a Power infinitely Superior to that of evil Spirits. Real Miracles that are contrary to the order, and exceed the Power of Nature, can onely be pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duced by creating Power, and are wrought to give credit to those who are sent from God. And when God permits false Miracles to be done by Seducers, that would thereby obtain Authority and Credit amongst men, the deception is not invincible; for 'tis foretold expresly, to give us warn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, That the man of sin shall come with lying Wonders, by the working of Satan, 2 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 2.9. and the heavenly Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine of the Gospel has been confirmed by real Miracles, incomparably greater than all the strange things done to give credit to Doctrines opposite to it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Jesus answered <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">We observed before, that the term <ns0:hi>Answered</ns0:hi> doth not always in the <ns0:hi>New Testament</ns0:hi> signifie a reply to a questi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on before propounded; but sometimes no more than a <ns0:hi>reply,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>beginning of another Speech</ns0:hi>; whether it doth so here or no, some question. Some think Christ here gives a strict answer to a question which <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> had pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pounded to him, about the way to enter into the Kingdom of God; which Question the Evangelist sets not down, but leaves to the <ns0:hi>Reader</ns0:hi> to gather from the Answer. O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers think that our Saviour knew what he won<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> say, and answered the thoughts of his heart. Others, That he onely began a discourse to him about what was highly ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary for him, that was a Master in <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> to understand and know; he begins his Discourse with <ns0:hi>Verily, verily,</ns0:hi> the import of which we considered, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 51.</ns0:note>, and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Tt. 5 3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> Except a man be born <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>from a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gain <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The word translated <ns0:hi>again,</ns0:hi> is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which often signifieth from above; so it signifieth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 31. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.17. and 3.15, 17. It also signifieth <ns0:hi>again,</ns0:hi> Gal. 4.9. <ns0:hi>how turn you again to these weak and beggerly elements?</ns0:hi> That it must be so translated here, and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. appeareth from <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> his answer in the next verse. But the expression of the second or new Birth by this word, which also signifies <ns0:hi>from above,</ns0:hi> may possibly teach us, that the <ns0:hi>new Birth</ns0:hi> must be wrought in the Soul <ns0:hi>from above by the power of God,</ns0:hi> which is what was said before, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>vers.</ns0:hi> 12, 13. the necessity of which our Saviour presseth from the impossibility other<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise</ns0:note>, he cannot see the kingdom of God <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">of his <ns0:hi>seeing the Kingdom of God</ns0:hi>; by which some understand the Kingdom of his Glory, (as the Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 18.24, 25.) others understand it of the manifestation of Christ under the <ns0:hi>Gospel-state,</ns0:hi> or the vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gour, power, and effect of the Gospel, and the Grace there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of. By <ns0:hi>seeing of it,</ns0:hi> is meant enjoying, and being made partakers of it, as the term is used, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 16.10. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 16.10. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 18.7. The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> promised their whole Nation a place in the Kingdom of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> as they were born of <ns0:hi>Abraham, Matth.</ns0:hi> 3.9. and the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> promised them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves much from their Observation of the Law, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Christ lets them know neither of these would do, but un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less they were wholly changed in their hearts and princi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples (for so much being born again signifieth; not some partial change as to some things, and in some parts) they could never have any true share, either in the Kingdom of Grace in this Life, or in the Kingdom of Glory in that Life which is to come. 'Tis usual by the Civil Laws of Countrys, that none enters into the Possession of an earthly Kingdom but by the right of Birth; and for the obtaining the Kingdom of Heaven, there must be a new Birth, a hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venly Renovation of the whole Man, Soul, Body and Spirit, to give him a Title by the wise and unchangeable Constitution of God in the Gospel, and to quali<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ie him for the enjoyment of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Nicodemus saith unto him, How can a man be born when he is old <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">By the answer of <ns0:hi>Nicodemus,</ns0:hi> it should seem that he was an old man; which is also probable, because he was one of the <ns0:hi>Rulers</ns0:hi>; he puts the cases as to himself; I am, saith he, an old man, how shou'd I be born?</ns0:note> can he enter the second time into his mothers womb, and be born <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Can a man enter the second time into his Mothers Womb, and be born? How true is that of the Apostle? 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.14. <ns0:hi>The na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God.</ns0:hi> What a gross conception doth <ns0:hi>Nicodemus,</ns0:hi> (tho doubtless a learned, as well as a great man) discover of <ns0:hi>Regeneration,</ns0:hi> as if it could not be without a mans Mother travelling in birth with him a second time? <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> his question, discovers a great deal of ignorance and weakness; but yet a great deal of simplicity and plainness in him; that he did not come, as the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> generally were wont to come to Christ, to catch him by captious Questions, but brought <ns0:hi>discendi pictatem,</ns0:hi> a pious desire to learn from him, and to be instructed by him. The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> had been used to study the <ns0:hi>Traditions of the Elders,</ns0:hi> and spent their time about unprofitable Niceties, as to the meaning of the Law; so were not at all versed in the great things which concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the Kingdom of God. The like Instance hath been in later Ages, the <ns0:hi>Popish Divines</ns0:hi> spending their time general<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly about nice School-questions, shewing themselves much ignorant of Spiritual things, and the great Mysteries of the Kingdom of God.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:333" />5 Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water, and <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi> the Spirit <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">To excite his Spirit and Attention, our Saviour again expresses the Authority of his Person; I say, and twice repeats the solemn Asseveration, Verily, verily, to shew the infallible certainty, and importance of what he propounds; that 'tis a truth worthy of his most seri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous consideration, and to be embraced with a steadfast be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lief. After this Preface, he declares, If any one be not born of Water and the Spirit, to rectifie the carnal conceit of <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> about Regeneration. In the third verse, our Saviour compared the spiritual Birth with the natural, and with respect to that, a renewed man is Born a second time. But in this verse, he expresses the cause and quality of the new Birth, that distinguishes it from the natural birth, and resolves the vain carnal Objection of <ns0:hi>Nicodemus.</ns0:hi> He speaks not of the Terrestrial Animal Birth, but of the Coelesti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al and Divine; that is suitable to that Principle from whence it proceeds, the holy Spirit of God. There is a great dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ference among Interpreters about the meaning of being born of Water. The <ns0:hi>Romanists</ns0:hi> and rigid <ns0:hi>Lutherans,</ns0:hi> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand the Water in a proper sense for the Element of Baptism, and from hence infer the absolute necessity of Baptism for Salvation: but the exposition and conclusion are both evidently contrary to the Truth. Indeed the new Birth is signified, represented, and sealed by Baptism, 'tis the Soul and Substance of that sacred Ceremony; and if our Saviour had onely said, That whoever is born of Water and the Spirit, shall enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, it might have been congruously understood of Baptism; because 'tis an undoubted truth, That all who are truly re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />generated in Baptism, shall be saved. But our Saviour says, He that is not born of Water and the Spirit, cannot enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; the exelusion of the un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sanctified, is peremtory and universal. And our Saviour shews a manifest difference between an affirmative and negative Proposition; when having declared, That whoever <ns0:hi>believes and is baptized, shall be saved</ns0:hi>; and coming to the negative, he onely adds, <ns0:hi>and he that believeth not, shall be damned,</ns0:hi> Mar. 16.16. The reason why he does not say, Who<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever is not baptized shall be condemned, is evident; for with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out faith, 'tis impossible to be saved; but without Baptism, even as the <ns0:hi>Romanists</ns0:hi> themselves grant, many have been saved. For if we consider the time when our Saviour spake these words, they acknowledg that Believers were not then obliged to receive the Baptism of Christ for Salvation; for our Saviour had this conference with him some years before his Death. And they hold, that before the death of Ch rist, Baptism was not necessary, neither by vertue of Divine command, nor as a means to obtain Salvation. Therefore the Believers that lived then, might enter into Heaven without Baptism. They also declare, that Martyrdome supplies the want of Baptism, and that Persons instructed in the Doctrine of the Gospel, and sincerely believing it, if prevented by Death without being baptized, their faith and earnest desire is sufficient to qualifie them for parta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king of the heavenly Kingdom. But if by Water here, be meant the Elementary Water of Baptism; the words of our Saviour are directly contrary to what they assert; for neither the blood of Martyrs, nor the desire and vow of receiving Baptism, are the Water of Baptism, which they pretend is properly and literally named by our Saviour. And certainly, if, as the Apostle <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> instructs us, 'tis not the cleansing of the flesh in the Water of Baptism that sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veth, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.21. 'tis not the meer want of it, without contempt and wilful neglect, that condemneth. By Water, then we are to understand the Grace of the Holy Spirit in purifying the Soul, which is fitly represented by the effi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cacy of Water. And this purifying refreshing vertue of the Spirit, is promis'd in the Prophecies that concern the times of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> under the Mystical Expression of Water. Thus 'tis twofold by <ns0:hi>Isaiah, I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and stoods upon the dry Ground,</ns0:hi> Isa. 44.3. And this is immediately explain'd, <ns0:hi>I will pour my Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit upon thy Seed</ns0:hi>; and the Divine Birth follows, <ns0:hi>they shall spring up as among the grass.</ns0:hi> In the same manner the effects of the holy Spirit are exprest by <ns0:hi>Ezekiel, I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be clean, Ezek.</ns0:hi> 36.25, 27. and presently after, <ns0:hi>I will put my Spirit within you.</ns0:hi> Our Saviour instructing a <ns0:hi>Pharisee,</ns0:hi> to whom the prophetical writings were known, expresly uses these two words, and in the same order as they are all set down there; first, <ns0:hi>Water,</ns0:hi> and then the <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> that the latter might Interpret the former; for Water and the Spirit, by a usual Figure when two words are employed to signifie the same thing, signifie spiritual Water, that is,<ns0:note place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Pateris liba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mus & a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                              <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>o,</ns0:hi> viz. <ns0:hi>a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                              <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>ress pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teris,</ns0:hi> Virg.</ns0:note> his Divine Grace in renewing the Soul; as when the Apostle says, <ns0:hi>in Demonstration of the Spirit and of the Power,</ns0:hi> to signifie the powerful Spirit. Thus <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> the Baptist foretold of Christ, <ns0:hi>That he should Baptise with the Holy Ghost and Fire,</ns0:hi> that is, with the Spirit, that has the force and efficacy of Fire to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fine us from our dross and corruptions. Thus our Saviour plainly instructs <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> of the absolute necessity of an inward spiritual Change and Renovation, and thereby shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the inefficacy of all the legal Washings and Sprinklings, that could not purifie and make white one Soul, which were of high valuation among the <ns0:hi>Iews. Entring into the Kingdom of God,</ns0:hi> is of the same importance, and sence with the <ns0:hi>seeing</ns0:hi> the Kingdom of God, in the 3 vers. That is, without Regeneration no man can truly be joyned with the Society of the Church of God, nor partake of the Coe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lestial Priviledges and Benefites belonging to it, here and hereafter.</ns0:note>, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God <ns0:hi>n.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 That which is born of the flesh <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That which was born of natural Flesh; for flesh some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times signifies the Man. So the Prophet saith, <ns0:hi>All flesh is grass</ns0:hi>; so <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 6.12. <ns0:hi>All flesh,</ns0:hi> that is, all men had <ns0:hi>corrupt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed their way.</ns0:hi> Or, That which is born of <ns0:hi>corruption,</ns0:hi> from vitiated and <ns0:hi>corrupted Nature</ns0:hi>; (so flesh is oft taken in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.4, 5, 8, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>)</ns0:note>, is flesh <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>is flesh,</ns0:hi> that is, it bringeth forth effects proportionable to the cause; a man purely natural brings forth natural Operations. Man, as man, moveth, and Eateth, and Drinketh, and Sleepeth. Corrupted man brings forth vitious and corrupt fruit, which often are called the <ns0:hi>works of the flesh,</ns0:hi> Gal. 5.19. Flesh here signifieth the whole man, whether considered abstractly from the adven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />titious corruption of his Nature, or as fallen in <ns0:hi>Adam,</ns0:hi> vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiated and debauched through Lust.</ns0:note>; and that which is born of the Spirit, is spirit <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">But that Man o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Woman who is regenerated by the Spirit of Grace, is spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual; he is after the Spirit, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.5. he is <ns0:hi>one Spirit with God,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.17. he is made partaker of the Divine Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.4. he <ns0:hi>doth not commit sin,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.9. No<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing in Operation exceedeth the virtue of that cause which influenceth it; so as no man from a meer natural Principle, can perform a truly spiritual Operation; and from hence 'tis absolutely necessary that man must be born of the Spirit, that he may be qualified for the Kingdom of Heaven.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>from a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> again <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">There is a twofold Admiration; that which is joyn'd with Infidelity, and that which is the effect of Faith. Our Saviour forbids <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> to marvel at the Doctrine of Regeneration, as strange and incredible, upon an imagina<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry impossibility supposed by him of the thing it self. But he that believes, will judg that supernatural work of the Spirit, whereby a sinful man is made a partaker of the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Nature, worthy of the highest Admiration. And what our Saviour had said in the general before, That a man must be born again; he now particularly applies to <ns0:hi>Nicodemus,</ns0:hi> with those of his order, <ns0:hi>Ye must be born again.</ns0:hi> For <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> would easily consent that the <ns0:hi>Pagans,</ns0:hi> and possibly the vulgar <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had need of Regeneration, to par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />take of the Kingdom of God; but that the Doctors of the Law, (of which number himself was) esteemed the Lights of the World, should be under the same necessity, was a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stonishing to him. Therefore, our Saviour to undeceive and humble him, saith, <ns0:hi>Ye must be born again,</ns0:hi> for that all are defiled with the corruption that is universal to man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kind.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eccl. 11.5. 1 Cor. 2.11.</ns0:note> The wind bloweth where it listeth <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The word which is translated <ns0:hi>Wind,</ns0:hi> being the same which both here and ordinarily in Scripture is translated <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> hath given Interpreters a great liberty to abound in their several senses. Some thinking that it should be tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slated, <ns0:hi>The Spirit,</ns0:hi> that is, the Spirit of a man breatheth where it listeth; and that our Saviours sense wa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>Nicode<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mus,</ns0:hi> thou needest not to wonder that thou canst not with thy sences perceive the spiritual new Birth, for thou can'st not understand the natural Birth. Others think it should be translated, <ns0:hi>The Spirit,</ns0:hi> that is, the Spirit of God blow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth where it listeth; but that seemeth not probable, because of these words, <ns0:hi>So is every one that is born of the Spirit</ns0:hi>; which will hardly be sense if we understand the first part of the verse, concerning the same Spirit, and <ns0:hi>vers.</ns0:hi> 12. Our Saviour saith, <ns0:hi>If I have told you earthly things, and you be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve not</ns0:hi>; they seem therefore best to understand it, who Interpret it of a <ns0:hi>terrene Spirit</ns0:hi> particularly. The Wind which is of a spiritual nature; and thus by their Translation it is apparent that our Interpreters understood it. So as, tho our Saviour speaketh of the motions of the <ns0:hi>blessed Spirit</ns0:hi>; yet he speaketh of them by way of Comparison, comparing it to the motion of the Wind, of which he said, <ns0:hi>That it bloweth where it listeth</ns0:hi>; not that it is its own mover, and under no government of the first cause; for the <ns0:hi>Psalmist</ns0:hi> tells us, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 148.8. <ns0:hi>That the stormy winds fulfil Gods Word</ns0:hi>; nor is any such thing competible to any Creature; but the Original of its motion is to us imperceptible.</ns0:note>, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">We can speak something philosophically to the cause of it, and can tell whither it bloweth from the <ns0:hi>East, West, North or South</ns0:hi>; but we cannot tell the particular place, where, or from whence it riseth.</ns0:note>: So is eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry one that is born of the Spirit <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">So every one, who is regenerated from the working of the Holy Spirit of God, is changed and renewed, so as we can give our selves or others no account of it in all points, as to the inward Operation, tho in the effects it be discernable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:333" />9 Nicodemus answered and said unto him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.52, 60.</ns0:note>, How can these things be <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> had before spoken, as if he thought it a thing impossible, understanding our Saviour of a carnal Generation, which he knew could not be repeated: Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceiving that he spake of a spiritual Birth, he is now posed at the Mystery of it; it being a thing, the Doctrine of which he had not been acquainted with. His carnal stu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pidity hindred his understanding the first Lesson of Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stianity, tho explained by the Sun of Righteousness: and his pride hinder'd him from confessing his Ignorance. He rather judges the Doctrine to be absur'd and impossible. The like darkness is in every unrenewed mind; <ns0:hi>Regenera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion</ns0:hi> being like that new Name, which none understand but those that have it.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Jesus answered and said unto him, Art thou a master of Israel, and knowest not these things <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Our Saviour doth not so much wonder at, as upbraid the Ignorance of <ns0:hi>Nicodemus,</ns0:hi> and all of his Sect, who went for <ns0:hi>Masters</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Teachers,</ns0:hi> and that in <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> who had the Law and the Prophets, and yet were ignorant of those things which were necessary to be known to every ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary persons Salvation. Will any say, But where was there any thing spoke in the Books of the Law and the Prophets about <ns0:hi>Regeneration,</ns0:hi> or a <ns0:hi>being born again? Ans.</ns0:hi> What other things could be meant by the <ns0:hi>Circumcision of the heart,</ns0:hi> commanded by <ns0:hi>Moses, Deut.</ns0:hi> 10.16. promised in <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 30.6. by the <ns0:hi>new Heart,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>new Spirit,</ns0:hi> promis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 36.25, 26. by the clean heart prayed for by <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid, Psal.</ns0:hi> 51.10. A Teacher in <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> should from hence have understood the necessity of a new, and of a clean heart; but the whole Sect of the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> were so taken up with the trifles of the <ns0:hi>Rites</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Traditions,</ns0:hi> and the works of the Law, that as to these spiritual things of nearer and much higher concernment to peoples Souls, they knew, and spake little of them.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7.16. and 8.28. and 12.49. and 14.24.</ns0:note> Verily, verily, I say unto thee, We speak that we do know <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Christ speaketh onely of himself, tho he speaketh in the <ns0:hi>Plu. Num.</ns0:hi> for in the next verse, he saith onely, <ns0:hi>If I have told you earthly things</ns0:hi>; he lets <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> know, that he spake nothing, but he was certain of.</ns0:note>, and testifie that we have seen <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">This he expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seth by two words, <ns0:hi>Know</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>See,</ns0:hi> which are terms expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sive of the greatest certainty of a thing imaginable; for the terms express a certainty of the mind, arising both from the rational deduction, and sensible demonstration; and herein our Saviour lets his Ministers know what is their Duty to teach unto people, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> What they know and have seen<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> those that think that the Doctrine of the Gospel would have no certainty, but for the authority of the Church, stand highly concern'd to reflect upon this Text.</ns0:note>: and ye <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 32.</ns0:note> receive not our witness <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Ye ought to believe what I tell you upon the authority of my Revelation; but such is the hardness of your heart, such your stubborness and unbelief, that you receive not my Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stimony.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 If I have told you earthly things <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">If I have spoken to you plain things, and in a plain stile, humbling my Phrase to your Apprehensions; and il<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lustrating Sublime, spiritual Mysteries, which in their own Nature are more remote from your apprehensions, by plain, and obvious Similitudes and Parables, and speaking thus, you understand and believe not;</ns0:note>, and ye believe not, How shall ye believe if I tell you of heavenly things <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">What would you do, if I should Discourse to you sublime and spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual Things, without these advantages for your understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.62. Eph. 4.9.</ns0:note> no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">No man hath so ascended up to Heaven, as to know the sec<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and Counsels of God, (for of such an as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cending it must be meant; (otherwise, <ns0:hi>Elijah</ns0:hi> ascended up to Heaven before our Saviour ascended); thus the Phrase is supposed to be used, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 30 4. None but Christ (who as to his Divine Nature came down from Heaven) hath ever so ascended thither,</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> the Son of man which is in heaven <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">even the Son of man, who was in Heaven, (we translate it, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi>) but the Participle <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, is of the <ns0:hi>Preterimperfect tense,</ns0:hi> as well as the <ns0:hi>Present tense</ns0:hi>; or <ns0:hi>who is in Heaven,</ns0:hi> by vertue of the personal Union of the two Natures in the Redeemer, as <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 20.28. we read, <ns0:hi>The Church which he hath purchased with his own blood.</ns0:hi> By reason of the personal Union of the two Natures in Christ, tho the properties of each Nature remain distinct; yet the properties of each Nature are sometimes attributed to the whole Person.
